inline.s: The fourth year of my exile to the ridges and seas was the year jihai; on the full moon of the seventh month of that autumn the Venerable Jing Yishan, Buddhist Regulator and resident master of Faxing Monastery, completed his sixty-first year. At that time the officials and lay believers of the city, with the monks of the four assemblies, each brought incense and flowers as offerings to congratulate him. It was the season of the summer retreat’s close and the Pavāraṇā, and the Venerable also held an Ullambana assembly to feed monks of the ten directions, following the old example of Maudgalyāyana, taking this as the way to repay his parents’ kindness and requite what can never be requited. I had just finished expounding the new Laṅkāvatāra for the assembly, and was making this very work my Buddha-task. Hearing that the Venerable had brought forth such a mind, I rejoiced and praised him, and said: The long life of worldly men never escapes self, person, and living being — what is called the mark of a long-lived one. Our Buddha does not take it up, nor does a monk abide in it. What the Buddha takes up is the life of wisdom; what he abides in is the Dharma-years. Hence the eminent monks of old spoke of a worldly lifespan and also of Dharma-years. Years are not the measure; rather, from one’s first receiving and keeping the precepts, three months of retreat, and a precept-body kept without loss, that is one Dharma-year. Because the reckoning is by Dharma-years and not by years, there are those advanced in age with few Dharma-years, and children with the long life of the aged. To prize Dharma-years is to take the precepts as root. With the precepts as root, the Buddha’s life of wisdom hangs upon them. Therefore when the root of the precepts is pure the life of wisdom is bright, and when the root of the precepts is firm the life of wisdom is long. The scripture says: If a person receives the Buddha’s precepts, he enters the number of the Buddhas. And since the Buddha’s life is measureless, it says that one has but to ascend the ranks of the precepts to obtain it at once. Is this not because one takes one’s own pure nature as Buddha and awakens to one’s own pure nature as monk? This is what is meant by continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom. Our Buddha taught the Dharma for forty-nine years; at the last he held up a flower and entrusted the treasury of the true Dharma eye to Mahākāśyapa. Through twenty-eight transmissions it came to Bodhidharma, who crossed the sea and first arrived at Wuyang. Earlier Guṇabhadra of the Song had brought the four fascicles of the Laṅkāvatāra and founded a precept platform there, and when Bodhidharma came he must have relied on it. When he transmitted to the Second Patriarch he pointed to the Laṅkāvatāra as the mind-seal. Later Zhiyao brought a bodhi sapling and planted it beside the platform, saying: A hundred and sixty years from now a great being in a fleshy body will leave home beneath this tree and proclaim the supreme vehicle. And the Sixth Patriarch did indeed begin his career there, as exactly as tally and notch. To this day the school has divided into five houses and its Way has covered the world, and all take this monastery as the first ground. Thus Bodhidharma’s Dharma is not extinguished and the Sixth Patriarch’s true body still remains. Is this not because the root of the precepts was firm and the life of wisdom prolonged, from ancient times to this and so on without end? Hence the scripture says: When a Buddha-son dwells in this place, it is the Buddha’s own enjoyment. Now the Venerable dwells in this place and governs these monks; to see the Sixth Patriarch as though alive — is this a small cause? When I first entered Guangdong and came to this monastery and knocked at its gate, I called twice and got no answer. Now I have lived here less than three years, and the monks are many and flourishing, all at once of one accord; young and old alike have brought forth the bodhi mind, and all is radiantly renewed in one’s eyes and ears. Is it that the Buddha-nature of these men did not exist before and now suddenly does? Buddha-nature is complete in every man; there was only no good teacher to open and guide them. But the work of opening and guiding lies in the one who leads putting it into practice with all his strength; then the four assemblies rejoice and are moved, like timely rain falling, flourishing luxuriantly without knowing why. Now the Venerable is sixty-one. On a single day he brought forth such a mind and did such deeds: by Buddha-work repaying his parents’ kindness, by pure precepts making the root of long life, and further drawing near to good teachers and following them in practice. If later disciples but look into the Venerable’s mind and imitate the Venerable’s conduct, from youth to age, from sons to grandsons, then transformation will beget transformation without end, a spring that never fails. If by any chance a Sixth Patriarch should arise and all be renewed as in the flourishing days of old, then the turning point of this Dharma’s revival lies again in this very day. The Venerable’s merit will be measureless and his life of wisdom endless; how could a trifling worldly lifespan compare with it? I therefore ordered his disciples the layman Tong’an, Ou Qihong and the rest, each holding incense and flowers, to proclaim these words again in congratulation of the Venerable’s long life.
Preface on Seeing Off the Chan Monk Yunsu Wen as He Returns to Jinshan

In my youth I cherished a wish to travel far, but illness prevented it. In the jisi year of Longqing I bought a boat and crossed to Jinshan. I loved that river of ten thousand li flowing on, a fist of rock propping up the sky, standing alone like a true man, towering with the bearing of one whose head is in heaven and feet on earth. The mountain’s master, the venerable Tong and Min, detained me, and I stayed two years. Many disciples followed me there. After each meal, with one or two lofty scholars, I would shake out my robe and wash my feet beneath the high bright moon: autumn river and long sky, one empty hue, as though treading on glass and looking into a hanging mirror. Since that parting more than forty years have passed; thinking of it in a daze, it is truly like a dream. I sank deep in the sea of pestilence for twelve years, drinking the smoke of the wilds and dining on poisonous mists, galloping through the burning house and sitting in scorching heat. Whenever memory stirred, my skin rose in gooseflesh and my very bones turned cool. It was this lone rock and long stream that served me then as pillow and rinsing water in my reed hut among the ramparts, a potent draught for scattering dust and dissolving vexation. A pity that it lies ten thousand li away, that kin and old friends are thinned and news is far and rare. I have often thought of the summit of Miaogao Peak and the stone of Sudhana — could the moonlight and the sound of the tide still taste as they did in those years? Yet there was no way to ask. In the late spring of the dingwei year I received the grace of pardon; I went to Duanzhou to call on the governor and received orders for Leiyang, to settle former matters. Returning to Wuyang, I called at the judicial office to await instructions and moored my boat on the bank of the Pearl River. It happened that a Venerable came from Yuzhang bearing a letter from the grand officer Mr. Ding. I opened the letter and read it eagerly, and learned that he was a grandson of Master Xuzhou Hong of Jinshan. Old feelings rose in me — truly what is called joy turned to anguish, sobbing into my kerchief. Alas, a man’s life is one generation; the years shift and alter, and looking back on the world it is all a dream. When my business was done I returned to the mountain, and Master Wen followed me to Caoxi. Now he speaks of going home; so I have set down old matters and recorded what I felt after our parting, as thanks to old friends. And I entrust him with greetings to the mountain spirits and the gods of the sea. I shall turn my boat back to the head of the Yangzi and revisit the old tales of the Three Mountains. May they drive off the Wind Earl to clear the river’s flow and sweep away the floating clouds to release the bright moon, and welcome me on Miaogao Terrace to sit in the Laṅkāvatāra chamber, speaking of the ocean waves of the storehouse consciousness and the realm of the dharma-body, and settling the unfinished case of Master Su and Zhang Fangping. Let Master Wen take this with him, and not let it sink away among rice baskets and clay bowls. If anyone asks, report for me that my beard and hair are now white, and that I no longer have the rice-and-gruel air of those years.
Preface on Seeing Off General Wu as He Returns to Yue

The General in his youth followed his father’s company into Guangdong, his ambition set on the field of battle. He crossed mountains and seas, smashing and pacifying bandits and pirates; there was no campaign he did not join and no battle he did not win. He looked on danger as level ground and on the deep abyss as a hillock, and he knew every island chieftain’s circumstances to the bottom. When the Japanese rose in trouble, those who talked of it looked on the vast sea as nine heavens to be climbed and on their flames as a fire to be entered. The Grand Commander of the Two Guangs, Lord Sima, deliberated daily with his staff, and all were at a loss. Then the General was recommended to go and scout; he obtained the whole truth, and the eastern affair was settled. When he returned to report, his old patron had already died, and the General’s merit found no way to speak for itself. He merely walked in the ranks and no longer dared speak of the affairs of the world. Yet high and low all knew the General’s ability; in the end none could raise him up. Whenever bandits tangled the passes, those in charge would all insist on the General, the General, and wished they could seat him at the head of the table. When the matter was over they would say: it was not that I could not do it. If anyone still spoke of the General, they too would say: the General, the General indeed. Thus the General’s fame bred envy and his ability brought disaster, and several times he barely escaped. Then those who had once called out the General, the General, again all took their own rule and measure as ample, and feared they had not gotten the General deep enough. Alas, such are the ways of the world; how could one dare speak of a great man’s business? When the southern barbarians violated the peace, all the meat-eaters turned black in the face. The General was then in prison. I thought that for one who could shoulder the burden of the frontier there was no second choice but the General, so I strongly asked that he be released. With much protection on every side he was placed in the vanguard. The General braved heavy seas and climbed steep ridges, fought battle after battle to Huafeng, stormed nests and broke lairs. General Yang knew him and so did not hide his ability, and the merit of heads taken and captives seized was greatest in the ranks. Yet the General, forgetting his own body, took a wound, and heart and spine were both spent; when the affair was done he nearly died of sickness. From this one knows that the General’s fate has been strange. The General by now knows well his own ill fortune, and so, bearing wife and carrying children, he has gone home to make a tour of the Five Lakes. The General is a man out of the dust, and I am not one who approves men out of temper or spirit. For when a mantis in rage raises its arms against a chariot wheel, who does not know its strength is insufficient? Yet to raise them in one burst of anger lies not in strength. By this I know the General, as the Nine Square judges horses: how could one exhaust his substance by mare and stallion, black and yellow? By this I am moved to sigh over the world’s skin-deep judges who fuss over the space between hair and color; such is not how I praise the General. On his way he passed Caoxi and came to take leave of me; we met by chance on the river and lingered two nights, so I made a poem to speak my farewell. Not that the General could soar aloft — words fail the meaning, and the laughter lies not in the words.
Preface to Master Zhou’s Awakening to the One

Master Zhou, named Xiyan, styled Ruyu, was a man of Taihe. For three generations his family had been orphaned and poor, and he was deeply filial. He applied his mind to the study of wind and water, and no famous lord or great man within the seas failed to bend his dignity and give him his heart, trusting him as the echo in a valley; for his words had proof and his affairs never went amiss, so men listened to him as to a voice, and his strange verifications were more than one. In late autumn of the jimao year he entered Caoxi with the prefect of Shao, Lord Ren. Caoxi is the dwelling of the Sixth Patriarch’s dharma-body. The mountain was first opened in the early Liang, when the spirit-monk Master Zhiyao said it was no different from Baolin in the western heaven, a peerless bodhimaṇḍa. I, seeing it decayed, privately doubted this, and put the question to Master Zhou. Master Zhou said: It is because its yin and yang do not follow the rule of the classic; it comes from the left and departs to the right, and so begins great and ends small. At that one word my doubt and blockage dissolved at once. From this I knew that Master Zhou’s talk of geomancy was not of forms alone. When he brought out his several essays on Awakening to the One, I saw the more that Master Zhou had gained the truth of his own nature, and only used forms to bring out its secrets. I once read Wang Wei’s poem: Mountains and rivers within the heaven-eye; the world within the dharma-body. The eye cannot admit the least mote of dust, yet he says it contains mountains and rivers; the dharma-body cannot be a mark of form, yet he says it embraces the world. Seen thus, how can one speak of it in forms and colors? This principle is subtle; truly it cannot be passed on in words, but lies in wondrous awakening. Therefore Master Zhou, in discussing mountains and rivers, always grounds them in true qi. True qi gathers and forms shape, as the human body must have blood vessels running through it; where the vessels meet and merge there is an acupoint. So while a man lives, if the needle finds the right point in illness it can open the gate of death and life; when a man dies, if the grave finds the right point in burial it can turn ill fortune to good. Such is the principle. It is said: Heaven and earth share one root, and the ten thousand things are one body. Thus the great earth is one form, yin and yang one qi, death and life one principle. Viewing the great earth as one qi, the eye sees no whole ox; viewing death and life through one acupoint, not a hair of the vessels is missed. If one looks at spring through a single leaf, the work of transformation does not change by a thread. From this I know that Master Zhou’s viewing of forms is not in the forms but in that which makes the forms. Originally the four great elements each pervade all and the five phases intermingle; all are rooted in nature and feeling. Because nature grew dim there was emptiness, the great ultimate; emptiness darkened and congealed into form, and the four great elements and five forms were thereby transformed. This is the root of form. Nature transformed and became form, and heaven and earth took their places. The tradition says: Bring about centrality and harmony, and heaven and earth take their places and the ten thousand things are nourished. This is the ultimate principle. Inner and outer five phases come forth from one; sentient and insentient share one body. When a man lives he moves and has knowing, and one who gains the center of heaven and earth is in his own person intelligent and penetrating; so when he dies he is still and has spirit, and one who gains the harmony of mountains and rivers brings fortune, long life, peace, and health to his descendants. Heaven and man join in virtue; the principle is most subtle. What is called burial that rides the living qi — is this not its meaning? From this I know that the world’s confusion over geomancy and its reckless talk of misfortune and blessing all come from not knowing the One. Master Zhou’s Awakening to the One is not merely a geomancer’s discourse, and his art is not spoken for those who seek forms; it is grounded in the body and seeks in the nature. Hence he named it Awakening to the One — how apt. Thus of the doctrine of forms: without Master Zhou before, the ancients’ secret could not have been brought out; without Master Zhou after, the reality of yin and yang could not be known. I say his book may be transmitted; so I have read it three times over, savored it deeply, and given it my mind. I write this preface to bring it out.
Preface Presented to the Old Man of Taihe

Of what place the old man was, no one knows. His beard was tossed back, his stature noble; a staff lay across his shoulder, and his feet had covered every quarter. Wherever he went he made the Buddha-work his own, pointing out delusion, so that those who saw his form turned their minds home and those who heard his voice unloosed their bonds — countless myriads beyond reckoning. Like clouds moving, like a bird flying, he drifted over the ridges and came wandering in Guangdong. I saw his sparse short hair, his two pupils bright as gleaming stars, his voice like a bell. I heard his talk blow like wind and his sharp point curl like lightning. Whatever the occasion, he manifested a body and spoke the Dharma; he discerned a man’s faculties and, by whatever method would bring liberation, by that method he freed him. To the Confucians he laid bare the purport of exhausting one’s nature; to the Daoists he opened the pivot of the dark and wondrous; to the Buddhists nothing he did was other than Buddha-work. Even devils and outsiders, iron-bellied and watery, all met his blade and had their points turned, and at the sight of his banner hushed their drums. Thus his Way was never given in vain nor his words uttered in vain, like Yang You’s archery or Shi Wen’s zither: he took up the arrow and it met the string, he touched the string and water sprang forth. Of such as these, too, there were hundreds of thousands beyond counting. Moreover his breast was open and wide, utterly without obstruction; he came without bringing anything and went without keeping anything, like those of old called the liberated ones who have attained non-obstruction. Was he not such? The old man and I sported in the vast wilds and roamed at ease in the broad plains, unaware that this body was in heaven and earth or that outer things were in this body. My spirit was glad and my heart drunk, as though dazed and foolish. Just as the old man was about to trail his staff and wander into the empty vastness, I suddenly awoke with a start and chased him to the water’s height; so I made a song to see him off. The song says: Cloud banners, ah, advance before; thunder drums, ah, without a sound. Wind fluttering, ah, blows my robe; trees dim and far, ah, hold their feeling. Your mind, ah, is unborn; what I long for, ah, is the spirit’s journey. I gaze and cannot reach, ah, to the sky’s edge; come again, ah, and startle my dream.
Preface Congratulating the Venerable Xian of Donghu, Former Abbot of Caoxi, on His Eighty-First Year

The Venerable Xian of Donghu, former abbot of Caoxi, was born in the dinghai year, and has now passed four hundred and eighty cycles of sixty days; the twenty-third day of the seventh month is the hour he left the womb. Among the great disciples of this mountain he alone is called the eldest in years. Moved by the Venerable’s virtuous teaching, which has long won the hearts of the assembly, each rejoiced, burned incense and scattered flowers as offerings, and with one accord bowed and asked me to set out the causes and conditions of his long life by way of congratulation. I gladly spoke these words for the assembly: The mark of a long-lived one arises from self, person, and living being; therefore our Buddha, the World-Honored One, rebuked it and did not allow it. Yet he also speaks of the Youthful Long Life, and again of the Measureless Long Life: why does he then single these out? The Youthful Long Life means that in youth one has the virtue of age; it is by virtue, not by years. The Measureless Long Life is by mind, not by form. For this mind is not old though it precedes heaven and earth, and does not end though it follows heaven and earth; it transcends the four seasons without shifting and embraces the ten directions without measure. Hence the true men of old who awakened to this mind are unworn through ten thousand ages and present through a thousand autumns. Thus our Buddha said of himself: I dwell on Vulture Peak, ever present and never extinguished. So too our master the Sixth Patriarch: his Way-bones are congealed and his dharma-body ever abides; how could this be something a body of bone and flesh can confine or marks of form can measure? Therefore we who are the sons and grandsons of the Buddha-patriarchs must simply awaken clearly to this mind, and not reckon long or short by worldly numbers. Looking through the thousand seven hundred men recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp, all come forth from the one vein of Caoxi; all of them awakened clearly to this mind. Hence mind seals mind, like a lamp continued through the long night, and they realized the fruit of neither birth nor death. This is truly to pass from birth into no-birth and through death to reach no-death. Not dying, the Dharma-nature is ever born; not being born, the true and constant is quiescent extinction. Thus in extinction there is birth, and no-birth is not unborn; in birth there is death, and death is not death. This is the true transmission of a thousand sages, the essential purport of the one mind. Seen thus, men share this one mind and the mind shares this one long life; there is no doubt. Now the Venerable was born at Caoxi, grew up in the Dharma-gate, and grew old in Buddha-work. Because he first made his own body the body of all, he can now take the long life of all as his own. Moreover the assembly of this mountain is a thousand men, each with his own mind, each mind with its own long life. Truly if we take the long life of all to wish the Venerable long life, then we take the Venerable’s long life to wish all long life; and so it turns and turns through endless time, like one lamp passing to a thousand lamps, lamp after lamp continuing without end. Thus the long life of the minds of all is truly endless, and the Venerable’s long life is measureless. From this one knows that eighty years are as one hair of a horse’s hide, one grain in the great granary. Now we gather the minds of all to wish the Venerable well, and we hope the Venerable will take this mind as his long life, so that his years be year by year as today and those who wish him long life be none of them fewer. Looking back, the day the World-Honored One held up the flower is not far, and the hour the Sixth Patriarch waved his whisk is not distant. Compared with the youth who has the virtue of age, this is as a gnat’s eyelash poured into the vast sea. The great assembly, hearing these words, rejoiced, bowed, and took this as their congratulation.
Preface Presented to Mr. Liang of Xingshan, a Skilled Physician

For eighteen years I was exiled to the ridges and seas, galloping through the burning wilds and drinking my fill of pestilent mists. This leaking body of mine is no metal or stone, and I saw it daily decaying as illnesses came on together. In the sixth month of the summer of the guichou year I happened to contract a carbuncle on my back as big as an overturned bowl; the pain was unbearable and the physicians were helpless. All who spoke of it recommended Mr. Liang. Mr. Liang by nature loved wine; whenever illness was reported to him he never counted his profit nor claimed merit at the end. Living in the village he was modest and yielding, with the manner of the ancients. When my illness was critical a man of the market told my servant: I hear the Venerable is ill; get Mr. Liang and he will be well at once. Before the words were done Mr. Liang arrived, as though invited by the spirits. I asked him to examine me, and he said: This is a honeycomb carbuncle. Its shape is like a bee’s cell, and a cell breeds three young each day; after some days they layer and invade the bone, and it cannot be cured. Happily it has risen early, and with medicine there is nothing to fear. His methods of treating it were many: when he spoke of pain the pain stopped, when he spoke of swelling the swelling subsided, when he spoke of decay the decay drained; following the illness his hand answered it and never failed of instant effect. His medicines used no metal or mineral, only common herbs. I watched him treat sores and saw into the viscera; his skill was like juggling balls, and he set a term for the cure as though a spirit aided him. At first, after he had treated me some days, someone recommended another physician, and Mr. Liang gladly yielded without a reluctant look; afterward, when the other could not cure me, Mr. Liang returned without a word of reproach. Thus one knows his art was high and his heart empty. At the time the attending physicians could not decide and urged prayers again and again, and only Mr. Liang was approved — truly a gift of Heaven. Moved by his curing my illness, I thought of the old saying: When a great man stands in the world, if he succeeds he becomes a good minister, and if he does not he becomes a good physician. Now the illness of the world is a hundred holes and a thousand sores, no less than my one body. Who will heal it? Even with the hand of Bian Que or Lord Yu, if one recommends them they are not necessarily trusted, and if trusted they are not necessarily employed — how much less where illness is concealed and the physician shunned: to seek the full restoration of the great harmonious vital breath and to win back the work of restoring life is hard indeed. Mr. Liang’s saving of men seems to have a spirit in it; his work of restoring life is more than one, yet he never demands repayment and accumulates hidden virtue. May Mr. Liang’s sons and grandsons extend his art to heal the world and the state, succeeding at a touch; then his bounty will flow without end, and not stop at his saving me today. Mr. Liang had until then no son. On the second day of the month after he healed me a boy was born, and all said it was the recompense of hidden virtue. So I gladly congratulate him and present him with these words.
Preface on Parting from the Scholar Chen Mingzhan

In the early Wanli years I begged food in the markets of Chang’an and met Mr. Chen of Yishan; at one glance among the crowd he recognized me as an odd man, and we became inseparable friends. I had earlier known that Lingnan had an Ou Zhenbo, who was then a guest in Yan with Mr. Chen. After that I withdrew from the world, and Mr. Chen too went on his official wanderings, and I heard no more of him. In the bingshen year I received the imperial order banishing me to Lingnan; in the second month I reached Wuyang, and inquiring after Mr. Chen found he had long since departed. It was then I met Mingzhan, his beloved younger brother. Mr. Chen of Yishan was heroic and outstanding, with a soaring thought of leaving the dust; Mingzhan was keen, quiet, and deep, careful and refined, calm and still, utterly without any worldly manner. I esteemed him. At each meeting he was silent and said nothing, yet nothing I said failed to please him. Later his elder brother, the court official Caifeng, hung up his cap and returned home and chose a western garden at Longjin, close to the Court of Imperial Entertainments Wang Weiwu of Fuqiu. From time to time they invited me to take vegetarian meals between the two gardens, and at every meal Mingzhan was placed first. Mingzhan followed the two elders and never went abroad; for the two elders’ integrity and righteousness were the crown of the age’s human relations, and not only honored in Lingnan. Mingzhan was born amid gravity, raised in it, and habituated to it; he not only knew what deserves gravity but was himself grounded in gravity. At eight he could set out the examination exercises, and at ten could recite the ancient prose and verse. When his father died, Caifeng looked on him as a son. When he grew up and Caifeng was at leisure, day by day he discussed with Mingzhan the figures of ancient and modern times high and low, and always pointed out what was weighty and gave it to him to blend his nature and habits; thus Mingzhan nourished and gained this gravity. No wonder Mingzhan would not stoop to trifle with the frivolous world. The Master said: If a noble man is without gravity he has no awe, and his learning will not be firm. Thus one knows that the learning of a noble man takes gravity as its root. Let me try to discuss it. Man’s nature is originally straight and simple, without falsity; only because former knowing leads the feelings and glittering show entices the will does the root perish and the substance change, the bright wane and the dark grow. Then one not only plants one’s root in the wrong ground but clings to what is not kin, and so daily drifts lower, stagnating in filth, until the ungrindable body is slowly worn and the unstainable substance is secretly soiled, and men grow dizzy and asleep, racing like fire and never turning back — and such are many. This is why the Sage prized drawing near to the humane, and why the Buddhists and Daoists value departing from desire. I have watched Mingzhan in this: ten years as one day, beginning and end as one thought, praise and blame as one mind; he does not change feeling with meetings and partings, nor divide his will with comings and goings. As for his bitter toil and plain fare, his filial piety and brotherly love, his deep sincerity — these are indeed his natural disposition; but truly they are grounded in nearness and habit. The tradition says: The heavy is the root of the light; stillness is the lord of haste. Hence in the Sage’s learning, if one gains the heavy the light follows, and if one devotes oneself to stillness the clamorous is transformed. Thus Confucius counted unrighteous wealth and honor as floating clouds, and Laozi held ten thousand measures of grain as a worn-out sandal. If one can gain this gravity, then poverty and success are one, death and life one strand, ancient and modern one thread. By this it is enough to prove that the learning of the outside-of-the-world is no idle talk, and that the school that came from the west is no eccentric marvel. Mingzhan and I have been friends for twelve years, and never once did a word pass between us on Chan; for Mingzhan long ago treasured this gravity, so what Chan would there be? Now we speak of parting, and I say no more than this. Let Mingzhan keep it in mind.
Postface to Fang Zizhen’s Subtleties of Go

In my youth I knew of Fang Zizhen, famous in childhood for his game of Go, though I never saw him. When I begged food in the markets of Chang’an, everyone I met praised him eagerly, and no one ever discussed his strengths or weaknesses. Privately I marked the man, and truly he was as the court historian Li Benning said: it was not the Go alone. When I was banished to the ridges and seas, in the late autumn of the bingwu year, Zizhen came to Guangdong with the provincial judge Xiao and visited Caoxi. At one meeting he was plainly a man after my own heart-mirror — how strange. He brought out his recent book, the Subtleties of Go, which he had set out with Huang Shifu; I could not fathom it. But when I watched him play against Lord Xiao, I knew that Zizhen’s Go advanced from the Way into skill. Let me try to discuss it. The Way is in heaven and earth; whoever gains its essence and makes its transformation spirit-like is called a sage. Of the Way and its virtue I will say nothing. As for the arts: Zuo and Ma are sages in letters, Zhong and Wang in calligraphy, Zhi and Su in cursive. Why only the arts? Skill is the same. So with the ball-juggler of Shiliao, the archery of Yang You, and Qiu’s Go — all have their records. Go is a way of contention. Whoever contends grinds against others for name, and grinding means temper triumphs while true virtue grows thin. Zizhen alone is not so. He is careful and refined, never taking his excellence as much; facing the board he seems to have no intent, meeting an opponent he seems not to know him. When the enemy is empty he must tell him the truth; when he holds the advantage he seems not to contend. His spirit is at leisure and at ease, laughing and proud in his own contentment; his breast is free and light, the board like clear water, the mind like the bright moon. He foresees the move and settles it beforehand; his spirit stirs and Heaven follows. When a guest departs he does not chase him; when the enemy comes he responds. From this one knows how very subtle it is. Some compare Go to warfare; I say Go may be likened to Chan, for it abides in non-movement while operating in movement. So I hold that Zizhen’s Go advances from the Way into skill. I observe Zizhen: it is not the skill alone, for the man is the same. Laozi said: Only because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him. Thus his character is rare and his skill is spirit-like. What then shall we call those who grimly wield the knife and cut? I do not understand Go, but having seen Zizhen play Lord Xiao, I am ashamed that I am not the Fushan who expounded the Dharma to Lord Ouyang over a game of chess.
Preface on Seeing Off the Venerable Jian Yin Ci to Abide at Dongchan Temple in Jinsha

Dongchan in Jinsha is an ancient monastery. It was revived by the Great Master Daguan; his disciples, the elder and younger brothers of the Sun family, began the work, and the court historian Lord Wang completed it. The Venerable Langya Yao was first obtained as abbot, and the adornments were complete. He then joined with like-minded men to form the Blue Lotus Society, reciting the Wondrous Lotus Sūtra from memory and observing the three studies of precepts, samādhi, and wisdom as their pure practice. Within a few years more than thirty could recite it. Formerly the Venerable Yao and the benefactors specially built the Hall of the Buddha-seed and invited me to retire there in old age. In the winter of the bingchen year I came east on my travels and saw its rules dignified and solemn, its retreat pure and clean, its four requisites ample and fine, its men and its setting both excellent, one of the most excellent bodhimaṇḍas of the Dharma’s last age. I praised it long. Then I settled the Great Master Daguan’s last causes and conditions and withdrew to old age on Mount Kuang; the Venerable Yao wept and begged me to stay, but I could not. In the second year after I entered the mountain the Venerable Yao departed through obstructive conditions, and all the benefactors looked to me to appoint someone to preside. Before long the Venerable Jian Yin Ci arrived, and the whole assembly joyfully and earnestly requested him. At first, because Guizong, his home mountain, was not yet settled, he returned to set it in order; now he goes at the summons. Passing by Wuru to take leave, I said to him with joy: How great is the Dharma-realm, which takes dependent arising as its doctrine. All dharmas are established solely by the one mind; the purity or defilement of a Buddha-land changes with the mind’s response, and its formation and destruction likewise. Therefore when our Buddha first attained right awakening at the bodhimaṇḍa, that ground was firm, made of diamond, because it was congealed by the diamond mind. Hence a bodhisattva’s practice must take this mind as the root of practice. What is called the diamond mind is the diamond precious precept spoken of in the Brahmā Net, named the mind-ground Dharma-gate of all Buddhas. Therefore he commanded a thousand billion Śākyas to transmit this Dharma, which is what is meant by appearing in the world for one great matter — namely, to transmit this diamond precept alone. This one precept is the condition for becoming Buddha; hence it is said, the Buddha-seed arises from conditions. We who are Buddha-sons, if we do not observe this precept, then whatever we establish, whether worldly or world-transcending, will all come to nothing, because it has no root. The rules of this society follow the three studies: among the three baskets the sūtras take the Lotus as their school, the vinaya takes the Brahmā Net, and the treatises take the Awakening of Faith. These three are all of the supreme one vehicle, revealing the purport of the one mind and the essentials of Buddhahood; nothing goes beyond them. This is a present, ready-made case. Now you go. If you hold the Buddha-mind as abbot, then that ground is made of diamond, body and mind are still, and you enter the Tathāgata’s chamber. If you take the Lotus as the Buddha-seed, then every look and every bow, every raised hand and lowered head, is wondrous practice, and every cause and condition is nothing but Buddha-work, utterly without weariness. If you illumine the one mind with wisdom and understand ignorance to the end, then afflictions do not arise and all obstructions cease of themselves; wherever you turn in daily use is true liberation. Moreover you have long kept the two chapters on Conduct and Vows and on the Universal Gate, devoting yourself to the pure karma. If you take great compassion as your mind, you will look on all as one body and view enemy and kin alike, utterly without marks of self and person. If you take Samantabhadra as your practice, you will give up body and life to serve the assembly, one drop of water moistening all alike — what private self is there? If you take the great perfect enlightenment as your monastery, then the ten directions assemble and each one is without doing; what then of the inheritance of sons and grandsons? If you so dwell, so hold, and so keep retreat, then at once you turn defilement into purity: the three studies are complete in one mind, ten thousand practices accomplished in one thought. As it is said: When a Buddha-son dwells in this place, it is the Buddha’s own enjoyment; ever present within it, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. Thus you will fail neither the benefactors nor your own one great cause of leaving the world. Hang these words in the Hall of the Buddha-seed; they may well serve as a broad long tongue.
Preface on Seeing Off Master Wuyan Dao as Abbot of Shaolin

The World-Honored One came forth from the land of India and sat on Vulture Peak, taking the utpala flower as the seed of bodhi. Later Bodhidharma took Shaolin in China as the first ground of bodhi, and the endless Dharma-stream of the ten directions has flowed out from there, source upon source. But as the branches multiplied the source grew muddled; therefore our Great Master Xue Ting gathered all the streams and returned them to one. His mind was great and his merit abundant. From then on the family seed grew generation after generation, and he who is unborn continued the family trade. Master Wuyan Dao inherited the Dharma-stream of the twenty-fifth patriarch, the Great Master Huanxiu Run, and is pushed forward by gods and men to preside over this house. All the great monks, the kṣatriyas, officials, and lay believers rejoice and praise him. I, come from the Nāravaṇa Cave in the east, also rejoice and join my palms, saying: Before the Buddha appeared and before the patriarch came west, this ready-made family estate was complete in every man. Because it was complete yet they did not know it, the yellow-faced and green-eyed one could not hold back his laughter, and specially came forth into the world to point it out to men. The millionfold assembly on Vulture Peak and the thousand seven hundred in the Transmission of the Lamp all turned their heads at a single call and suddenly knew what they originally had. Thus the one word knowing is the gate of all wonders. Ah, but the Buddha-patriarchs originally have no actual dharma to give men; who would expect that every man’s diseased eye sees flowers in the air, and then would pluck the flowers and seek fruit? Was this the Buddha-patriarchs’ mind? Thus the one word knowing is also the gate of all disasters. If we do not scrape the golden lancet again and again, how shall we continue the family trade? Alas, it is hard. Yet the Buddha-patriarchs take the Dharma-realm as their home, the great earth as their estate, and empty space as their measure: if they do not establish a single mote they cannot manifest a body, and if they establish a single mote they cannot save beings. Now you, with your bare body, shoulder the whole estate and drag a hundred rivers back to their source — how is this easy? You are about to go. Listen closely, listen closely, and bear it well in mind. If you do not establish a single mote, you fail the Buddha-patriarchs; if you establish a single mote, it is not what the Buddha-patriarchs hope of you. Take good heed.
Preface on Seeing Off the Lecturer Yangya Qing, Who Paints the Portraits of the Patriarchs

Long ago the World-Honored One dwelt three months in Trāyastriṃśa, and King Udyāna could not stop thinking of him; so he ordered craftsmen to take sandalwood and go carve his image. Śāriputra, fearing the workmen were common stuff and could not do justice to his wondrous beauty, by his spiritual power transformed thirty-two men, each to model one mark; when the marks were done they asked to bring it back to the royal city, and those who saw it took it for the living Buddha. When the World-Honored One came from the heaven he bowed to it and said: After my extinction, through you I shall save countless beings. And the image too let down its hand in reply. Hence all carving, painting, and every kind of adornment throughout the ten directions began with that sandalwood. Ah, was this the Buddha’s doing alone? My thought is that all the patriarchs share one body, one wisdom, and the powers and fearlessnesses likewise. Hence it is said: The mind is like a skilled painter, painting out all forms. Forms can be painted — but spiritual powers, wondrous functions, and the work of saving beings: how can they be painted? This I had long felt to be lacking, until I read Master Da’s account of Ding’s painting of the patriarchs’ portraits, and his sending off Master Qing to seek a painting. Then I knew that spiritual powers, wondrous functions, and the work of saving beings never depart from the samādhi of a single hair’s tip. Alas, Śāriputra exhausted his spiritual power and needed many men to make one image; now Ding, by the wondrous power of non-doing, manifests many bodies from one hand; Master Qing, in a single thought, completes the work of saving beings; and Master Da, in a snap of the fingers, suddenly makes the dharma-body spread abroad like clouds rising in the cold sky or reflections spread over autumn water. Is such wondrous function the natural spiritual power of things, or does it come of causes and conditions meeting? If the viewer can face it without doubt, he will believe that each man’s own nature is originally complete in just this way. You are going; do not weary of the flourishing of many works. Should many bodies again appear from one body, they will fill the void and pour light over the great earth, and still not depart from Ding’s single hair’s tip. Take this with you, and give my word to him.
Preface Congratulating the Venerable Chaoru Ying, Left Elder of the Bureau of Monks, on His Abbacy of the Great Temple of Compassion and Longevity

In the first years of the Sage Son of Heaven’s reign, when he was still young, the Eminent Mother toiled and worried in rearing him, and thinking that the ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain, the heavy vessels of the world, were reposed in him, she considered how she might above repay his great virtue and below bless the common people. So she reduced her offerings and cut down her table, and from her own funds built the Great Temple of Compassion and Longevity, hoping to rely on the Three Jewels’ protection and secretly shelter the far corners of the land. When the temple was done, the monk Chun of Gufeng was chosen abbot. He dwelt there three years and departed this life, and the emperor appointed his grandson Ben Zai to the office of Left Elder of the Bureau of Monks and to continue the temple’s affairs. Master Zai held the post twelve years: above he prayed for the emperor’s long life, below he received the four quarters’ comers, never wearying morning or evening. Truly the cloud of compassion and the rain of Dharma that filled the whole region all flowed out from this. Yet the Master poured out his loyalty and spent his strength, exhausting himself; because his affairs were many and his duties heavy, his body labored and his spirit dried, and the four elements sickened together. Though worn to bones he still could not bear to lay down his charge. Chan Master Daguan, passing by Cishou as conditions led him, saw him and cried out in alarm: How have you come to this? We may indeed value forgetting the body for the Dharma, but what of the great matter of birth and death? The Master silently wept a few tears and said: It is not that I cling to empty fame; I only think of the imperial grace so weighty and the incense and fire without a support, and so I drag on. The Master then asked who could bear the temple’s affairs, and he at once named his disciple the monastery supervisor, Chan Master Yuanying. He asked to see him and was overjoyed, saying: Is this not one who comes riding on vow-power? He had him loosen his robe and sit at ease, and judged him as the Nine Square judged horses, saying: This one is equal to a thousand li. Happily we have this child; what is there to worry about? When Master Zai heard this he resolved clearly on his own, and the next day reported the matter to the Eminent Mother, who approved it. The decree went down to the Grand Master of Rites, and Ying was ordered to retain the office of Left Elder of the Bureau of Monks and to be the third abbot. All the great teachers of the famous mountains rejoiced when they heard, and asked me to praise it, saying: Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, takes the Dharma-realm as his home, the three studies of precepts, samādhi, and wisdom as his estate, the spreading of Dharma and benefit of beings as his business, compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity as his model, and teaching, principle, practice, and fruit as the ropes that bind it. When the three studies are complete, the four minds are perfect, and the four cords are drawn taut, the teaching flourishes. This household is dwelt in by no-mind and held by no-self; it lets causes and conditions decide advance and retreat, and follows what fits the faculties in taming and subduing. This is the able business of a man of the ultimate, how could an ordinary man reach it? Therefore in the age of the true Dharma the four cords were drawn taut and the Dharma-way flourished. Looking closely at the patriarchs, whether young or old, at a single word they succeeded to the estate. In the age of the semblance Dharma the teaching flowed to the eastern land; through Han to Tang there were men in every generation, leaf after leaf fresh, flowers and fruit abundant — though it is said there was no fruit. As for the last age, those who flower and fruit are few, because the teaching and principle remain while practice and fruit are lacking, and the net is half loosened; how then shall one bind the family estate and fish up gods and men? Now we have entered the last age by more than six hundred years. When the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvāṇa, sixty trillion bodhisattvas vowed to influence and spread the Dharma in the last age, and he further entrusted the Buddhadharma to kings and great ministers. Hence generation has succeeded generation, and our own state honors this teaching and respects its men, high and low as one body; and to our Eminent Mother, who has spread the Three Jewels beyond former ages, with jeweled palaces and dark-blue halls scattered like chessmen and stars. This temple alone is the great spectacle of the world: the inexhaustible Dharma-store issues from it and all merit enters through it. It is the pivot of the Dharma-gate and the resting hut of good teachers. Whoever holds its charge upholds the ropes of the great teaching and is the lookout of the four seas; this is no small matter. Master Ying was only twenty when he took the post of monastery supervisor, and all the temple’s many affairs he took upon his own body: he did not favor himself, did not shrink from toil, did not decline resentment. He did not know that his body had a world, nor that his mind had a body; without knowing or recognizing, he responded at large without contrivance. This is what is called young in years and old in virtue, solid without and empty within; forgetting contrivance he is like no-mind, responding at large he is like no-self, reckoning neither gain nor loss he is like one who lets conditions be. This is truly the able business of an abbot. Was not what Chan Master Daguan called one who comes riding on vow-power just this? I have privately said that Master Zai is the boat and Master Ying the water: if the water is not piled deep, it has no strength to carry a great boat. Master Ying has already been able to carry his master for ten years with proof; how could he not carry himself? Master Ying, take heed. May you reach its truth and tread its reality, be a true son of the Buddha and preside over his house, and with this body and mind pray for the compassionate long life of our Sage Lord, like heaven and earth covering all without end. If it be so, then the shadows of the incense banners move, the sound of bell and drum flies, the pagoda and hall span the sky, and the chimes and clappers ring without pause day or night — all of it the hour when the broad long tongue turns the Dharma-wheel. Take good heed.
Preface Presented to the Venerable Dalun Duan on His Abbacy of Guangji Temple

North of Rājagṛha there is a great monastery called Guangji, where the great teacher Master Baozang expounded the Dharma. The Master first hid on Zhongnan and brought the mind-seal to light; afterward he brought his disciples, Master Shuang Song Ping and others, and stopped here, planting the great Dharma-banner, and gods and men gathered in crowds. The Master sat on the lion seat and Master Ping took charge of the abbacy, receiving the four quarters, and his fame tipped the seas. For more than thirty years the Master’s Dharma-years reached eighty, and his Way-wind grew greater with each day. Master Ping then took leave of illusory conditions and departed, and again his disciple Master Duan continued the mountain gate’s affairs. The elders of the capital, the Venerable Ruian of Longhua and others, all rejoiced and begged a word from me in praise. I have heard that the Buddha dwelt in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, in the Jetavana monastery, with twelve hundred disciples, each commending what he esteemed; and so the elder was named Empty-born. Empty-born asked the Buddha where he dwelt, and the World-Honored One told him: One should bring forth the mind that dwells nowhere; one should not bring forth the mind dwelling on form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharma. And he said: Thus should one dwell, thus should one tame the mind. Where then does he dwell? Yet is it dwelling in no-dwelling? I have also heard that the Buddha dwells in the storehouse of great light, and secretly with the twelve great beings spoke the perfect sutra-gate, saying: Take the great perfect enlightenment as my monastery; body and mind dwell at peace in the wisdom of equal nature. This is what is meant by dwelling in the field of quiescent extinction and practicing the non-doing. Again, is it dwelling in something dwelt in? Yet the Venerable received the Dharma directly from Master Baozang, and the Master received the Dharma from Chan Master Dachuan, who held the true command of Linji: a raised eyebrow, a blink, a staff, a shout — and the five teachings are gathered at once, a thousand gates meet in an instant, man and setting both taken away, principle and fact both forgotten. How can one measure this by the monastery of the royal city or the monastery of perfect enlightenment, weighing coarse and fine, better and worse? If the Venerable truly presides with this Dharma, he will be able to continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom and above repay the state’s kindness — truly what is called a Buddha-son’s abbacy, excellently transcending all existence. When the elders heard this they were all greatly delighted, and take this single leaf to greet the Venerable. Let not the Venerable think me the sick man of Vaiśālī, no hand to snatch the bowl. This is the preface.
Preface on Seeing Off Master Fangshan Yingchuan’s Phantom Wandering

The phantom man went wandering in the capital and met Master Fangshan in the great field of illusion, and we became friends in heart. Afterward the phantom man departed with illusory conditions, and Master Fangshan entered the gate of the great liberation that is like an illusion, relying on the field of quiescent extinction and manifesting all illusory affairs; he raised the great canon in the dragon palace and received the wondrous offerings of gods and men. The phantom man was just then hiding his shadow in the Eastern Sea, occupying the long void and the great valley, contending for mastery with mist and cloud, elk and deer. Master Fangshan heard of it and was glad; he came at once, staff in hand, seeking me out in the far northern wilds. The phantom man took him by the arm and wandered with him: we climbed the Diamond Peak and entered the Nāravaṇa Cave, rode the firm raft and floated on the light of the ocean-seal, groped in the void and commanded the ten thousand forms. When weary we spread the jade grass and lay in the long forest; when hungry we drank the ambrosia and dined on chestnut and thorn. Sometimes we would drum on our bellies and prop our chins, slap our thighs and leap like sparrows, drink the whale-waves and swallow the vast sea, shout at the great clod and breathe out the long wind, until the ten thousand apertures rang together and the separate streams raced in haste — never knowing that you and I were in the cosmos, or that dawn and dusk were sun and moon. How much less could floating light and phantom shadows, dust and heat-haze, mark the measure of the great clarity. Master Fangshan was glad and forgot to return; before he knew it two watches had passed and the four seasons were an instant. Then Master Fangshan sprang up and said to the phantom man: I have heard that the land of no death is not for the mayfly to conceive, and the broad desert is not for the midge to know. Is it true? I wish to die there with you. But my illusory conditions are not yet exhausted; I must leave you for a while. In the end we shall join hands and return together. The phantom man slowly answered: Ha, is that so? Do you make a thought of coming and going? Try to look: when a wisp of cloud rises, the great void is filled with it; when a mote of dust lifts, the whole earth is gathered in it. Undivided, it spreads everywhere, and the rich rain falls abundantly; undispersed, it is complete, and the mountains vie in beauty. Seen thus, no dharma ever departs from where it rises. Take good heed, and make no thought of coming and going. Yet the flower in the air bears fruit, and the clouded eye is fooled by it; the water bubble is strung as a pearl, and the foolish child is deceived. Go then, and try to flick it away and scrape it clean; if the pearl breaks and the cloud is removed, do not forget our covenant of clasped arms. I vow to die with you in the Nāravaṇa Cave.
