Record of the Restoration of the Venerable Wan’s Stūpa Court at Shijing Mountain in Zhuozhou

Long ago I read the canon and came upon the vow-text of Great Master Si of Nanyue, who vowed that his flesh body might abide forever, upholding the Buddhadharma while awaiting Maitreya. This was already most rare. Later, when I traveled to the upper capital and let my eyes wander over the Lesser Western Heaven, I saw how mighty the stone canon was. In the Daye era of the Sui there was a monk of Zhiquan Temple in Youzhou, the Venerable Jingwan, who could not bear that the three calamities should destroy the kalpa and the great Dharma be submerged; wishing to keep the Buddha-seed unbroken, he began to carve the stone canon in plates and sealed them in Baidai Mountain west of Zhuozhou. The mountain has seven caves, and cave after cave was filled. From the Daye era to the twelfth year of Zhenguan of the Tang his vow was not yet ended when he died. His disciples, the four masters Dao, Yi, Xian, and Fa, carried it on through five generations, and still the canon was not complete. Through Tang and Song there was no generation without such men; and in the Zhizheng era of the Yuan the Korean monk Great Master Huiyue had still not finished the work. The whole course of the matter is recorded in the various steles and banners at Yunju; only in our Ming have we heard nothing of it. Why? Ah, if the man is not there, the Way does not walk in vain; the Buddha-seed arises from conditions — is this not its meaning? At first the Great Master Daguan Ke, in the autumn of the bingxu year of Wanli, visited me at the Nāravaṇa Cave, then traveled north to Yunju and came to the Venerable Wan’s stūpa. At one look his tears fell like rain, as though a lost son had come upon his parents’ grave. He embraced the banner and wept bitterly, lingering long before he went. He traveled south to Emei, and on returning to Jintan, to repay his parents’ kindness, he finished writing out by hand the Lotus and Śūraṅgama sūtras. Six years later, in the sixth month of the renchen year, he came to the capital and commissioned the imperial equerry Mr. Xu Yan to make a precious case, intending to send it to the Ten Thousand Buddha Stūpa at Luya; and so he rested awhile at Tanzhe. When the Eminent Mother, the Compassionate and Holy Empress Dowager, heard of it, she sent the attendant minister Chen Ru with offerings of vegetarian provisions. Chen Ru went with the Master again to Yunju and paid reverence to the stone canon at Leiyin Temple. Then suddenly light shone through the cliffs and ravines, and when they lifted the stone of worship in the hall, the stone had a casket, and in the casket a silver box; the silver box held a golden box, which contained a golden bottle with three relics, bright as diamond, as though they were the original possession. The whole assembly marveled, grief and joy mingled. Afterward they paid reverence again to the Venerable Wan. At that time the stūpa court had already been sold by the temple monks to a powerful family, and the Venerable’s bones would soon share a nest with foxes and hares. The Master was deeply grieved and at once redeemed it with the gold that the Compassionate and Holy One had provided for the vegetarian offerings. It was not enough; the palace eunuch Yang Ting had his disciple Xu Fadeng help complete it. The Master then went to escape the heat on Shangfang Mountain, and I too came from the Eastern Sea and called on him at the Tusita Court. When we spoke of this he slapped his palms and grieved. In the time of a meal the Master’s senior disciple, the Venerable Mizang Kai, arrived with the deed of redemption and with Xu Yan. The Master sprang up for joy and at once drew me along to Yunju to pay reverence and praise. Braving rain and mud, we arrived at the day’s end. Walking three times around to the right, we stood silent before him, and a stern living air came forth. He sighed and said: This one is indeed undying. Moved by the encounter, he and Mr. Xu together donated gold to buy several mu of land as a fund for keeping incense and fire. Master Da then commanded me to record the matter. But who am I? Assenting, I said: The whole great earth is the permanent dharma-body; only a man of the ultimate can know it. A single mote of dust holds the sūtras of a great thousand worlds; only the eye of wisdom can see it. With such a body to speak such a sūtra — this Dharma is most profound, and few can believe it; and to believe it, how is that easy? Therefore our Buddha, the World-Honored One, through vast kalpas looked over the ten directions and found not a mustard-seed’s worth of place where he had not given up body and life for beings’ sake, seeking the place of this Dharma; at last he obtained it, and at once on the tip of a single hair manifested a Buddha-land and in a single mote of dust turned the great Dharma-wheel. Thus all the words and letters of the twelve divisions of the three baskets are our Buddha’s own bone, blood, heart, and marrow. Therefore it is said: Wherever this sūtra is, one should raise a stūpa and make offerings; there is no need to place relics therein, because the Tathāgata’s whole body is already there. Hence one who can uphold this Dharma has repaid the Buddha’s deep kindness. At the assembly on Vulture Peak the Buddha wished to entrust this Dharma to someone; at that time gods and men were a million, yet not one dared draw breath and shoulder it. Were not this great assembly heroes and great men? Yet though they had personally received the Buddha’s charge and taken the Buddha’s kindness to heart, still they hung back and shrank in fear; they must wait for the sixty-two billion host, countless as the sands of the Ganges, to well up from the earth — why? And the Buddha allowed only five hundred years after his nirvāṇa, and no more; how much less to wait for Maitreya through the three calamities and to the end of the kalpa? This shows how hard it is to uphold the Dharma. Seen thus, one who can raise a single thought of deep resolve to protect the Dharma is protected and remembered by all Buddhas. For without the Dharma the Buddha could not have attained right awakening, and without the Buddha the Dharma could not save beings; without beings one could not understand one’s own mind, and if the mind is not understood one cannot protect the right Dharma; and if the Dharma is not protected, how can one repay the Buddha’s kindness and be called a disciple? Truly when the Buddha is extinguished the Dharma is extinguished, and if the Dharma abides the Buddha’s body abides forever. The Buddha with his constant body occupies the Dharma-realm and builds his great work; and as for guarding its borders, there are surely many means. Our Great Master of Nanyue held it all together by his vow; yet he does not compare with the Venerable Wan, who put it into action. Still, though the Buddha’s work is great, without Nanyue none could raise its cords; and though Nanyue’s vow was vast, without the Venerable Wan none could continue the work; and though the Venerable Wan was lofty, without Huiyue none could carry on his will. Alas, to follow and repair is easy; to begin from the wild is hard. To continue the flame and pass the lamp there have been men in every generation; but as for one who stands towering in the Dharma-realm, one beginning and end, sharing its sorrow and its joy, with bitter heart and deep thought succeeding to the Tathāgata’s family estate — leaving aside Ānanda and setting aside the Youthful Long Life, there is only the Venerable Wan alone. Ah, his merit is great; beings through the end of the kalpa receive his gift. Were it not for him, the Buddha himself would wear the barbarian’s coat. Did he come personally receiving the secret seal, or is he one of the sixty-two billion? How vast was his vow-power. I sigh that in this turbid world few know him, and so he who does is precious; and as for one who both knows him and does him honor, again there is only my Great Master Daguan alone. He and the Master were truly what is called the meeting of a thousand years in a single morning and evening. Alas, if the world does not know the Venerable, it does not know the Buddha; yet if it does not know the Master, how can it know the Venerable? I say the Venerable’s mind is the Buddha and the Venerable’s bones are the sūtra; the mark of the broad long tongue neither perishes nor is born. The Buddhadharma does not decay, resting on the Venerable’s bones; bones and Dharma-realm are each other’s beginning and end. Now the Master and the Venerable have brought the dead to life and clothed bone with flesh, restoring what had passed; this is to split a mote of dust again and bring forth the sūtra of the Dharma-realm. Is this a small cause? Alas, the Venerable’s bones are entrusted to the Master, and the Master’s mind is carved in stone. Whoever reads this writing hereafter without shedding tears is like a man who hears of his parents’ heart’s blood and marrow and does not change countenance — most assuredly no true son. I hold that we disciples have tears, and they must surely be shed upon the Venerable Wan’s bones.
Record of the Relics in the Leiyin Cave of Shijing Mountain West of Zhuozhou

In the twentieth year of Wanli of the Ming, the renchen year, the first day of the fourth month being gengyin, on the fifteenth day, jiachen, Chan Master Daguan Ke came from Mount Wu and escorted the Dragon Son back to Tanzhe. When the Eminent Mother, the Compassionate and Holy Empress Dowager, heard of it, she sent the close minister Chen Ru, Zhao Yun and others with funds for vegetarian offerings. On the first day of the fifth month, gengshen, on the twelfth day, xinwei, the Master, with his attendants Dao Kai and Ru Qi and the imperial equerry Xu Yan and others, came to the Leiyin Cave of Shijing Mountain. The cave is where the Venerable Jingwan in the Daye era of the Sui carved the stone canon. The Master saw that the images and furnishings in the cave were choked and the stone canon eaten away, and ordered Mingliang, abbot of the Eastern Yunju Temple, to clear them. That day light shone through the cliffs and ravines and wind and thunder shook the earth. The next day they opened the stone of worship in the cave; beneath the stone was a hollow, and in the hollow a stone casket a foot square, its face carved with the words: In the twelfth year of Daye of the Great Sui, cyclical year bingzi, fourth month, dingji, eighth day, jiazi, within this casket are placed three relics of the Buddha, with the vow that they abide through endless kalpas. Thirty-six characters in all. Within were stored four or five pints of sacred bones, like stone marrow, with a rare fragrance. In the midst was a silver box an inch or so square, containing a small golden box half an inch, containing a small golden bottle like a broad bean, in which were placed three relics of the Buddha like millet grains, purple-red, like diamond. The attendant Kai asked that they be brought to the Master, who joyfully bowed and praised. Then he wrote a letter to Zhao Yun, entrusting Xu Fadeng to petition the Eminent Mother, the Empress Dowager. The Empress Dowager was delighted, fasted and kept vigil three days, and on the first day of the sixth month, jichou, had them brought into the Palace of Compassionate Peace and made offerings three days. Outside the small golden box she added a small jade box, and outside the jade box again a small golden box, an inch or so square, set within the silver box, as an adornment. She brought out fifty taels of silver from the treasury and had a great stone casket made to enclose them all. In the twentieth year of Wanli, the renchen year, the first day of the eighth month being wuzi, on the twentieth day, dingwei, they were again placed in the stone hollow, with the vow that they abide through endless kalpas, and that life after life, when conditions meet, they be seen again. He commanded the monk Deqing to record the matter. Deqing, with single mind and joined palms, said: The relics are what our Buddha in the causal ground, when he first brought forth the diamond mind and poured forth the light of precepts, samādhi, and wisdom, steaming and perfuming the leaking and impermanent and transforming the three karmas, brought into being; and there is the difference between the whole and the part of the produced body and the dharma-body. From his first awakening until habit and outflows were utterly exhausted and the three virtues were perfect, whatever appeared according to conditions — the marks and light of his flesh body, blazing like a jewel mountain, a purple-burnished mass of Jambu gold — his three karmas and six senses, within and without translucent, so that this impermanent body realized the diamond substance. Therefore at the great parinirvāṇa the great disciples and the hosts of gods each took sandalwood and black agaru as the pyre to burn his body, and skin, bones, blood, flesh, hair, nails, and teeth flowed with the firelight, each one transformed into a diamond seed, utterly firm, unburned by fire, undrowned by water, like quicksilver on the ground, every drop round. These are called relics, which means bone-born. This is the produced body, seen only in part. Hence their color follows skin, bone, blood, flesh, hair, nails, and teeth, and there are red, yellow, white, and black, each color different; small ones and large, round ones and straight, like dew, like pearls, like millet, like beans. And because they are perfumed by three things — meditative concentration, walking the Way, and vow-power — there are those that move and those that do not, those that manifest wonders and those that do not. Those of meditative concentration are congealed and ever still; those of walking the Way turn about in bottle and plate and never rest through the ages; those of vow-power answer whenever sought. As he said: I dwell on Vulture Peak, ever present and never extinguished — is this not the whole dharma-body? Ah, what Yongjia called the illusory empty body being the dharma-body, was it an empty saying? Seen thus, all living beings possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtue-marks, but because they are perfumed by delusive thought, ignorance, and karmic action they become impermanent and decaying bodies. Yet in daily use before one, thought after thought secretly flows, and the true light alone is exposed, bursting into eighty-four thousand pores, each ray of light shining without end; and this impermanent body and mind become the permanent diamond. If this light were poured out to illumine the whole earth, then all mountains, rivers, grass, mustard seeds, and motes would be nothing but the true substance of Buddhahood, ultimately firm, unmoved and undecayed, each one a dharma-body relic — how could there be any measure? But because they are seen according to the power of beings’ minds and conditions, the whole produced body of the World-Honored One yielded only eight bushels and four pecks. And it was divided into three, and the heavens, the human world, and the dragon palace each took a share to build stūpas and make offerings. What was spread among men was the stūpas built by King Aśoka with great spiritual power, sending ghosts and spirits as envoys, filling Jambudvīpa; and in our China those that can be counted on the eye are nineteen, and Yu-wang at Mingzhou stands first. Is this too what the two wisdoms perfumed? And what the spirit-monk Kang Senghui sought at Changgan in Jinling — is it not what vow-power perfumed? As for the eminent monks of every generation, wherever the three studies were perfect there was often such a thing, but these are merely called firmness-seeds. I have said that China was of old called the Red County and Divine Land, and its people have mostly the faculties of the great vehicle, and our Buddha’s relics are countless; how could those it reached be only ten or so? I privately doubted this. Then I read the Record of the Responses of the Relics and saw that in the Sui the nun Zhixian obtained one relic. When Emperor Wen was first born the nun took him up and raised him; when he grew up and bore the great work he thought to repay the nun, and she only entrusted him with the relics she had kept, saying: You should be the compassionate father of all under heaven and revive the Buddhadharma; with these build stūpas everywhere, and that is enough. What repayment do you owe me? The emperor received them as a command. Of the famous mountains and stūpas and temples within the realm today, most are therefore from the Great Sui. I say: could the relics hidden in this cave be those that the Venerable Wan personally received from Emperor Wen’s hand? Or are they the canon upheld by our World-Honored One’s vow-power, showing a small part of his true body, wishing to let beings suddenly see the whole? Now our Master Ke came once and the relics at once appeared, and through him they were given to the nation’s mother — was this too brought about by former conditions? Otherwise, why did response and calling meet and shine so clearly? I say that in the time of the Three Wu the Buddhadharma had not yet reached Jiangzuo, and yet the relics — by what cause were they earlier in the ground, their light soaring to the heavens? The monk Senghui came seeking the light, and Wu still thought it strange; but when he spoke of these relics and begged for them with a twenty-one-day vow they arrived, and the men of Wu turned from marveling at the strange to reverence and faith, and the spread of the Dharma-way began from this. Generation succeeded generation for more than a thousand years, until our Sage Ancestor and Divine Progenitor revered and served it beyond a hundred ages and relied on it for Jinling’s eternal foundation as the settled capital. To this day the stūpa’s light shines, adorned and wondrous, equal to the Buddha’s body — is this a small matter? Moreover this stone canon was the Venerable Wan’s riding of Nanyue’s vow-wheel to await Maitreya, passing through the three calamities and to the end of the kalpa, not merely a hundred million ages. These relics had long been buried; now our Master Ke came once, and without seeking they appeared. Our Eminent Mother dwells in the ninefold palace, and without expecting it they came of themselves. Is this not our Buddha by his great vow-power protecting the Three Jewels and appearing in season to prolong our ancestral shrines and bless the common people forever without end, causing the right Dharma to spread and the Buddha-seed to be unbroken? And if we examine the stone canon the Venerable Wan carved, from Sui to Yuan it was more than six hundred years and only half was done; by our Ming it had fallen utterly silent. Is this not our World-Honored One showing a small part, like one leaf of a flower revealing the boundless spring, wishing to cause beings from this canon to continue far into the end of the kalpa the Tathāgata’s dharma-body and life of wisdom? Otherwise, why was its appearance so very easy? Therefore I, Deqing, have been able to record the whole course in detail to show it to later ages, so that those who see and hear may know the sage does not respond in vain and that a response must have its cause. Is it a mere nothing? This is the record.
Record of the Permanent Estate of Mingyin Temple in the Great Capital

Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, descended in spirit to Vulture Peak to teach the Dharma and save men; and among his disciples, none who had not left family and family honor for pure practice did he save, and none who had not entered the unborn did he let dwell. Hence he dwelt nowhere fixed, only admonishing them: One meal at noon, one night beneath a tree, to show that this remnant life is a traveler’s lodging, going on and never returning. He had no thought of the human world’s high and broad dwellings and rich and fine fare. Later, to benefit the royal city, the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada wished to ask the Buddha to teach, and so begged the garden of Prince Jeta and built a monastery to invite him; he did not grudge spreading gold over the whole ground, and thus the many-storied halls and lecture pavilions were opened, and the assembly’s dwelling in retreat began from this. Yet they still went out daily to beg, and the four requisites were never rich or fine. Afterward, for the old and sick who could not go begging, a permanent estate was established. This permanent estate was set up for the old and sick — how could it be intended for the affairs of today? As the teaching flowed east, jeweled palaces and great monasteries were scattered like chessmen and stars, their smoke and fire within sight of one another, their bells and drums within hearing. But the further from the Sage, the more the original intent was twisted. Therefore Chan Master Baizhang rose and greatly revived it, establishing the pure rules to flank and support the vinaya, hoping to return to the first system. Alas, those who dwell in them — are they all men who have left family honor, put away glory, and hold pure practice to awaken to the unborn? Hence those who build are not always Anāthapiṇḍada, those who answer are not necessarily like the Buddha, and those who dwell are not necessarily all old, sick, and unborn. Therefore it is said: If you do not receive guest monks, my Dharma will perish. Then it is not only no field of blessing but turns into a sea of poison. At this I cannot but weep till my tears wet my lapel. South of the capital there is a temple called Mingyin, formerly named Sansheng, built by the Great Master Yunya. The Master was born in Baoding; at seven he put on the black robe, and at eighteen he wandered abroad, visiting good teachers everywhere. At the bodhimaṇḍa of Mount Wu the robbers had first seized its throat and cut off the road of refuge; earlier there had been the Great Master Wuzhu Ding, who with young forest karma opened a bandit lair at Jiulu Ridge and built a monastery called Longquan Temple for travelers to rest, and there Mañjuśrī’s Dharma-way greatly prospered. The Great Master at twenty assisted Master Ding in opening it out, and his merit was great — was it not a former vow? The Master dwelt at Longquan ten years before entering the great capital; there he ascended the platform and received full ordination, and at once established Sansheng Temple to receive the four quarters. Five years later he was selected as Great Master, and by imperial command ascended the jeweled seat and transmitted the vinaya Dharma for many years, his Way growing ever more prosperous. In the third year of Wanli he restored Mingyin Temple; ten years later the Great Master entered extinction, and five years after that his grandson the Venerable Qing of Yangya continued the estate. But the Master, by his learning and conduct, was weighty in his age, and holding Longquan he taught the Dharma and inwardly moved the Eminent Mother, who donated gold to restore his temple, granting it the name Huguo Mingyin, the merit being rooted in the Great Master. In the autumn of the renchen year of Wanli I came to the royal city as conditions led, and met Chan Master Daguan at the Great Temple of Compassion and Longevity. The Venerable Qing came with the Chan Master to see me and said: Mingyin was founded by my ancestor. Seeing the monasteries of every quarter, I have seen that those who dwell in them often do not embody the intent with which the former sages built them; and as for those who sell themselves to keep the rules, what shall be done with the burden of their karma? I wish to make this a permanent estate forever. From now on, at this mountain gate one meal shall be shared with all; the worthy may dwell here, the old and sick be at peace here, travelers be received here. Whatever the permanent estate requires, the officers may increase but not decrease. My sons and grandsons may dwell but not divide it. Whatever profit is given may be public but not private. Its fields may be kept but not sold. May the incense and fire of generation after generation be bright as sun and moon, to exalt the Three Jewels, repay the Buddha’s kindness, and pray for the emperor’s long life, drawn out without end. He asked me to record the matter. Hearing it, I rejoiced and leaped up and praised him, saying: You take the Tathāgata’s mind as your abbacy and Baizhang’s mind as your permanent estate, and cause those who dwell here after you to take non-discrimination as wondrous practice. Should the whole world hear the wind and rise up, every place would be no less than Jetavana, and the excellent counsel of the right Dharma might be seen again today. How can the Venerable’s merit be measured? Let me set down his mind and carve it in firm stone, to show it to later ages.
Stele Record of the Opening of the Guanyin Cave on Jinping Mountain

China’s famous mountains are mostly full of wonders, and the Taihang is the overseer of heaven and earth. From Shouyang to the mountains and sea, its fine qi gathers in the capital; hence the whole stretch of the Western Hills about the capital is studded with jeweled palaces and Brahma halls like overlapping scales, all of them human labor dressing the work of transformation. As for what is naturally wonderful and needs no carving, and whose beauty surpasses the common run, there is only the one place of the Guanyin Cave on Jinping Mountain. The mountain lies about a hundred li west of the capital, and the cave sits in its breast, one range of three hollows like the eyes of Maheśvara. Within, all is exquisite and congealed, water and milk taking form, a thousand postures and ten thousand shapes that cannot be named. The mountain’s force encircles it; rare flowers and strange herbs bloom like a brocade screen. A single stream takes its source from a deep valley, winding and turning, clear and still at the mountain’s foot; hence its crowding peaks stand tall like blue lotuses rising from the water. The elders relate that in the mist and clouds they have often seen the Great Being Guanyin appear, and so it was named. In the spring of the guiwei year I wandered with my staff among famous places and fasted in the Three Studies Cave. Lord Wang Jue of the timber office came to see me and spoke of this, and so I went to look. At one sight I loved it deeply. The Lord then asked to open it out and first donated thirty mu of land as a beginning for incense and fire, and built a tea hut to help travelers. At that time I was weary of wandering in the world and had no leisure for the work, so I entrusted it to my Dharma companion the Venerable Zhen Yu of Jiufeng to preside, and at once went east over the sea. Afterward a certain official came by command to supervise the office’s affairs and became a strenuous founder-benefactor, and the heads of the office helped with one mind. They opened the ground and gathered workmen, hollowing the empty and filling the solid, bringing down the high and leveling the low; after several years they made cliffs and banks of several tens of feet, and outside the cave built two bays of meditation rooms. What was bramble is now a jewel ground. In the autumn of the renchen year, carrying my bowl in the royal city, I passed this place again and sighed deeply, saying: Truly the setting changes with the mind, and the Way lies in human effort. I have heard that the Great Being Guanyin, perfect and universally responsive, appears everywhere; for she abides where response and calling meet, as the moon appears when the water is clear. Moreover every man is originally Buddha, but without practice he cannot become one; every place is a bodhimaṇḍa, but without work it cannot be seen. This mountain is indeed numinous, but had Lord Wang and the others not relied on causes and conditions to build it ardently, then even seven-jeweled adornment would have been left to the brambles; how could one hope to turn brambles into a monastery? Now the sound of bells and Brahma chanting speak prajñā together, and the grey cliffs and stone walls all reveal the dharma-body. Those who hear are not deluded; those who see awaken at once. Those who realize perfect penetration through this place cannot be numbered. The merit of those who initiated, gave, labored, and helped will be forever without end, to pray for the emperor’s long life and spread the wind of compassion in an unbroken line. The Daoist Haiyin, not forgetting its beginning nor reckoning its end, made an inscription, saying:

The great earth is the dharma-body; originally not an inch of soil. The towering grey cliffs — every eye beholds them. The falling perfect sound — in itself it has no voice. The rushing, flowing waters — every ear hears them. Every place is a bodhimaṇḍa, nowhere is it absent. Those who have the strength turn gold into soil. The Great Being of Perfect Penetration manifests a body according to kind; how could she favor only this place, pitying only sentient beings? The cave is originally empty, yet a thousand wonders and ten thousand shapes are the very root and feature of perfect penetration. When the time had not come, it lay long buried in dust; when the season met, at one plan it opened. Its sound shakes the gates of heaven; its light soars over the great earth. The merit of seeing and hearing is inconceivable. Above, we pray for the imperial plan and the peace of the altars of soil and grain. May the Sage’s long life have no bound, through a thousand autumns and ten thousand years.
Stele Record of the Repair of the Great Cixuanwen Temple at Fangshun Bridge, Lower Court of Fenglin Temple on Mount Wu (with Inscription)

Mount Wu is the bodhimaṇḍa of Mañjuśrī, where ten thousand bodhisattvas teach the Dharma within, responding and transforming without fixed rule, with many kinds of numinous wonder. From the Yongping era of the Han, when Matanga left his traces, down through the Three Kingdoms and Six Dynasties, and through Tang, Song, and Yuan, the records of the reverence paid by the emperors, empresses, consorts, and princesses of successive dynasties can be pointed to one by one. Our Emperor Chengzu, the Civil Emperor, invited the Great Treasure Dharma King to dwell there, and thereafter jeweled palaces and Brahma halls increased in honor year by year. When our present Sovereign came to the throne, in the early Wanli years, our Eminent Mother, the Compassionate and Holy, Proclaimer of Culture, and Reverent Empress Dowager, to assist the late emperor and safeguard the imperial person, greatly made Buddha-offerings, beginning with the famous mountains of the world at Mount Wu. She invited twelve eminent monks, with Chan Master Erhu of Fenglin Temple as first seat. The Master’s name was Deyin and his style Chetian; he was a man of Taiyuan in Shanxi. From first to last his career and his practice were bound to the mountain, and he was long renowned within and without. The Eminent Mother built Fenglin Temple for him to dwell in. When the temple was finished, because Mount Wu is a thousand li from the capital and the mountain recesses run several hundred li, she further established a reception temple beside Fangshun Bridge in Mancheng County of Baoding Prefecture, named the Great Cixuanwen, and set aside more than ten qing of temple-supporting land to guard the incense and fire and make it last forever; and she ordained the novice Mingli as his attendant. The Master’s Way was honored beyond the world and his fame reached the inner court; the imperial grace was weighty beyond the common run. Such men as the court providers Mr. Xu and Mr. Wang of Qingming, and the gentry of the time, and the Grand Marshal Lord Wu, all deeply honored the Master; hence wherever his bodhimaṇḍa was, it became a monastery, with morning bells and evening chanting, incense and fire scattered like stars. All this was to pray above for the emperor’s long life without bound and to safeguard the imperial plan for a hundred million years. Truly it was all our Eminent Mother’s boundless compassionate grace, yet in truth it was the Master who moved her to it. Now this place supports the monks’ flesh bodies and makes firm their life of wisdom; how can its merit and blessing be reckoned by number? Our Eminent Mother’s compassionate grace is as broad and deep as heaven and earth, and this merit too will share its long endurance; surely there are ghosts and spirits guarding it. Those who hereafter come near this place and hold this ground — will they not trace whence the Sage’s mind came, and dare they forget the kindness of ruler and parent and incur the blame of ghosts and spirits? When the temple was completed he commanded the monk Deqing to record the matter. I reverently bow my head and make an inscription, saying:

Most perfect is the prime of earth, from which the ten thousand things draw life. Towering Taihang is the warp of heaven and earth. Lofty Qingliang is the holy bodhimaṇḍa; a host of spirits make their lairs there, resting on the north. Without, it guards the fence; within, it arches to the divine capital. Jeweled palaces and Brahma halls are monasteries everywhere. It was our Eminent Mother who nurtured the emperor’s virtue; whatever she did was all for the realm. She built this famous monastery to invite the Brahma companions. They come from the ten directions like clouds, like a wall. To cultivate the life of wisdom one must rely on the flesh body; no need to carry a bowl, for the fragrant store is full. The land is like rich fat; the assembly is like clouds. The holy mind of our Eminent Mother turned earth into gold. May this ground abide forever, and this merit alone be undying. We pray for our emperor’s blessing, enduring as heaven and earth.
Stele Record of the Permanent Estate of the Ten Directions of Ciguang Temple on Mount Funiu

From the time he descended at Kapilavastu monasteries began to rise; when the white horse came east the monks’ dwelling was first opened. The codes of reverence and repair through the ages, the groves of the ten-direction ocean-assembly, the rules by which Baizhang broadened the vinaya system, and the practice of tempering the demons set up at Mount Funiu — all were nothing but the refined cultivation of the one mind and the taming of the three karmas. Those who came like clouds took the Dharma as their mind; those who dwelt in retreat made harmony their business. As the world declines and the Way grows faint, and we are further from the Sage, not only does the Dharma have no specialized gate, but men keep the mark of self, so that the admonitions of the two benefits remain empty and the conditions of the four requisites are spent in vain. This is why the World-Honored One knitted his brows and why men of the ultimate gave forth sighs. Reverently thinking of our

Eminent Mother, the Compassionate and Holy, Proclaimer of Culture, and Reverent Empress Dowager, bearing the power of her compassionate vow, manifested the body of the state’s Grand Mother, exalted the Three Jewels, and raised the great Dharma-banner, so that the famous mountains within the realm all became jewel grounds and the fair traces of the world all turned into monasteries. She donated funds from her own table and commanded the close attendant eunuch Jiang to build Ciguang Temple on Mount Funiu as a ten-direction ocean-assembly monastery, and set aside two estates of farm land at Taihechuan and Heiyubao for the perpetual offering of incense and fire. She appointed the monk Zhiming to preside over the temple’s affairs. Zhiming had first studied in the capital under Master Baozhu of the Western Tiantai Temple, and was known in his day for ascetic practice.

The Eminent Mother had long revered him. On the day Zhiming set out the Master admonished him, saying: You, a single foolish common man, have undeservedly received the compassionate command; searching your heart, will you not bear it always in mind? Take the Buddha as your mind, the Dharma as your life, the ten directions as your permanent estate, and the assembly of monks as your monastery. In eating you must share with all; in any matter you must consult the assembly. Take virtue as your leader and public honesty as your steward. Do not cling to yourself, do not slight others. Day and night, through the six periods, temper the three karmas and practice the ten thousand practices with vigor, shutting off all other conditions. So shall you pray for the emperor’s long life without bound and repay the compassionate grace through endless kalpas. Do not forget my words today. Zhiming kept the precepts and practiced accordingly, and reported this to the Eminent Mother; and she, taking thought for the long road, further commanded the eunuch Lord Jiang to manage it, hoping the bodhimaṇḍa would vie in light with the two halls and the monastery stand level with Mount Niu. The beginning and end of the work are already fully recorded in the merit stele; now I record together the means by which Zhiming held the estate, to set a model for the monastery and be a lasting admonition for later men. Those who dwell there in the future shall take this admonition and admonish those after them again, like the passing of firewood and flame, forever without end. This is the record.
Record of the Repair of the Mountain Spirit Temple at Zhifu (with Inscription)

Ten li or so southeast of the prefectural city of Deng there is Mount Zhifu, and on the mountain a spirit called the Marquis of Floating Blessing; of this there is no record to examine. I have surveyed the world’s geography: roughly, from Kunlun it turns east, and the Bohai pours into it. The sun rises from Fusang and light and shadow rise and fall; the three mountains of Penglai loom faintly in mist and cloud, their palaces dimly gold and silver, and the immortals mostly dwell there. It is called the land of no death. For this the First Emperor of Qin traveled east to Huangchui and to the end of Chengshan, and climbed Zhifu to look toward the morning sun and carved a stone to record it. Thus this mountain was first enfeoffed long ago. Fifteen hundred years have passed since, and though comings and goings have succeeded one another, its old story is as clear as the palm. The common people take refuge in it and sacrifice at the seasonal feasts, and the mountain too produces excellence and shows its numinous power: wind and rain come in season, so that creatures are free of plague and the year’s grain ripens. Hence the temple offerings are unbroken. The Complete Reality Daoist Gao Changqing dwelt there nearly thirty years, reached ninety, and had the face of a child. Many of the prefectural men are given to refined pursuits; General Qi above all served it well. Seeing the spirit hall fallen, the General donated a sum and gathered the people and workmen to renew it. The work began in the autumn of the dinghai year of Wanli: a hall of four bays with side corridors and covered walks complete, finished within a year. Changqing once came staff in hand to Haiyin and asked me for a record; so I made this inscription, saying:

Transformation’s embryo, and the great clod is formed; mountains and rivers gather beauty, nourishing spirits and producing excellence. This great abyss, to which a hundred rivers return: Kunlun points east, and Zhifu towers. The First Emperor of Qin came up; Penglai loomed faint. The Han emperor sought spirit men with boastful, blurry words. Only the mountain’s spirit endures through a thousand autumns and ten thousand years, settling our land and state. A hundred blessings without end; the people are blessed and the grain is gathered in. Jeweled palaces and pearl towers are repaired and made new. Whale bells and alligator drums roar at dawn and hum at dusk. We pray for our emperor’s blessing, high as the mountain, deep as the sea.
Stele Record of the Practice and Dharma-Origin of Chan Master Wuji Xin, Abbot of Jixiang Court in the Capital

Chan Master Wuji was a descendant of the twenty-sixth generation of Linji. His dharma name was Mingxin, and he was a son of the Song family of Shahe in Shunde. At eight his parents gave him up to leave home, and he took Master Shen of Tianning in the prefecture as his teacher. As he grew a little he grieved over birth and death; at thirteen he asked his own master for leave to go on pilgrimage, and went to Mount Niu and entered the great fire, practicing with vigor and enduring hardship, tempered day and night for more than twenty years. Though he felt the dust of toil fall away for a time, he had not yet entered awakening. Then he returned to visit his family and came to Shangzhanping on the western mountain of the prefecture, utterly beyond human tracks, and hid there six years with one meal a day, until all thoughts suddenly ceased. Before long he visited good teachers everywhere, went north to the capital, ascended the platform and received full ordination, and again hid on the middle peak of Mount Yin, keeping his shadow out of sight three years, feeding daily on acorns and chestnuts and concentrating on meditative contemplation. Then suddenly mind and setting were both empty, faculties and dust fell away at once, and he was abruptly awakened, aware that his very substance had nothing to rely on. The Great Master Cuifeng, holding the true command of Linji, was teaching at the capital gate; the Master went to seek his confirmation, and the occasion met and matched. Soon after he took leave and hid in the Jixiang Chan Monastery at Jinshan west of the capital, taking long nurturing as his aim, firmly holding his solitary hardness, calm as though he dwelt nowhere, wearing rag robes and eating the food of nestlings for more than twenty years. The palace eunuch Lord Zhang Xian and others heard of him and came to see him, and donated gold to renew the Brahma halls; and scholars from every quarter advanced daily. Before long the Master thought of his home mountain’s desolation and sighed with the wish to return. He went west, staff in hand, to the ancestral stūpa, to give thanks for his liberation. Then two or three elders came forward and said: Our ancestral lord Xuzhao inherited afar the true vein of Caodong, and his character-lineage runs: Hong, Zi, You, Ke, Fu, Yuan, Shan, Qing, Ding, Hui, Yuan, Ming, Yong, Zong, Jue, Xing. Now it is about to end; how will you continue it? The Master then spoke a verse: Wisdom and ability broadly reaching; wondrous function without fixed direction. Emptiness held, the ultimate reality: the ancestral Way, honored incense. The disciples assented and recorded it. Before long he returned to Jixiang and hid his shadow from the world, receiving the four comers, and his Way-wind grew greater day by day. One day, without illness, he called the assembly, spoke a verse, and calmly sat upright and passed away. It was the seventh day of the second month of the second year of Wanli. His worldly life was sixty-three years, his Dharma-years more than thirty. His ordained disciples and others carried out the cremation and gathered the Master’s sacred bones, burying them in the Hidden Stillness Stone Cave on the western ridge. His disciples all studied with Master Xiaoshan of Shaoshi and succeeded to the Caodong blood-line; and he who now teaches at Tianning on the old mountain, through the Great Master Ruian of Longhua, brought the Master’s record and asked for a memorial. So I have set it out according to the facts, saying: I have heard that our Buddha, the World-Honored One, having finished saving beings, taught the Dharma forty-nine years and yet said he had not spoken a single word, and at the last twirled a flower as the purport of the special transmission. From the time Kāśyapa smiled on Vulture Peak, the twenty-eight in the western heaven and the twenty-three in the eastern land gave forth what cannot be measured or limited; and yet he never allowed its branches to separate — there is deep meaning in this. After six transmissions, from Nanyue and Qingyuan beneath them, it divided into five houses, whose gate-and-court arrangements and establishments differed, like ears, eyes, mouth, and nose in one body: their uses differ, but can one make the body different because their uses differ? Seen thus, what was scattered was never one, and what returns is never two; how then can one change its pointing-home because the gate-and-court uses differ? Yet those of later ages who awakened each entered by their own gate; and as for the occasions of Caodong and Linji, they have not faded to this day. Why is that? One who has the true eye should, as before the Buddha appeared and before the patriarch came west, raise his brows and look: then the one assembly on Vulture Peak and the nine years at Shaoshi are all leftovers. Thus prince and minister exchange places, staff and shout fly back and forth, heaven and earth are covered and contained — talk of matching the occasion and secretly witnessing is no more than lightning in the great void, a spark from a flint, while the lion plays. If the Chan Master in the samādhi of quiescent extinction gives one shout that deafens the whole earth, and all who hear it are not terrified, then one may say: I offer this deep mind to the dust-realms; this is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness. Otherwise, by what Dharma would one continue it? This is the record.
Record of the Repair of the Guanyin Hermitage on Wu Mountain (with Inscription)

Southwest of Lao Mountain, by the sea, a host of peaks and ridges rush and stand together; and one peak that rises above the vast waters is called Wu Mountain. The elders relate that long ago an eminent monk hid there cultivating and awakening to the Way, and so it was named. In the Jiajing era of the Ming a monk named Jinwu made a thatched hut on the site and dwelt there, and restored three bays of the hall of the Great Being Guanyin, with side rooms flanking it left and right: the windows swallow mist and cloud, the door draws in the long waves, and one sits as though on a lotus beholding the moon in water. When the hermitage was done he asked me for a record. Rejoicing and praising, I made this inscription, saying:

The Great Being of Perfect Penetration manifests a body wherever she is; within a single mote of dust she turns the great Dharma-wheel. The sea of suffering has no shore; it races and swallows the waves of consciousness. The Great Being looks on it as an image in a mirror. I rely on the Great Being’s samādhi of illusion, and have also come here to realize samādhi. Every grass and every tree belongs wholly to the dharma-body; this is called the permanent estate, passing on the inexhaustible lamp, shining through the dark. Fire breaks out in water; a lotus is born in fire. This is the true Dharma; through endless kalpas I take refuge. Such is my praise; may those who see and hear alike ascend the other shore.
Record of the Repair of the White Cloud Hermitage and the Jade Emperor Hall on the Summit of Jufeng (with Inscription)

Lao Mountain lies southeast of Jimo, its roots spreading over two hundred li, straddling the plain and pillowing on the sea. Ridges rise and fall like dragon and snake winding; grasses join in fragrance and tall groves are dense. In hidden and secret places, stone chambers and rock niches: hence in the past many true men and lofty scholars built their traces there. A host of peaks encircle it, and in the midst one summit stands out, called Jufeng. It occupies the seat of the two Laos, piercing the upper heavens above and looking down on the boundless below, the most wondrous of all. On its summit is a hermitage called White Cloud, long known as an ancient monastery. It fell into ruin. In our

Ming dynasty, in the Jiajing era, the Complete Reality Daoist Guo Yiju revived it; his disciple Li Yangxing continued the estate, and down to his grandson Gao Laide it was greatly renewed. They hewed stone along the cliff and walled the hollows of the rock; cinnabar chambers and round halls were complete on both sides, and in the middle they built three bays of the Jade Emperor Hall. A certain Mr. Zhou of the county, with the Lai provincial censor Lord Liu Zhuozhai, helped complete it. It was managed for years and only finished in the jimao year of Wanli. In the summer of the guiwei year I wandered by the sea, exploring its fair prospects, staff in hand on that summit, when I happened to choose a dwelling at Taiqing; and he asked me for a record. I have heard that among the sea mountains there are three mountains, called Langyuan, Penglai, and Fangzhang, whose palaces are all of gold and silver, and where the immortals dwell. Hence those who live in the dust and dwell in turbidity, hearing of them, feel their spirit fly and wish to leap free and rise aloft, straightway leaving the world; but when they arrive, what do they see? Because the ocean is vast and shoreless, and without wings none can reach the end, they give free rein to wild fancy — how can it be so? It is but joy and weariness contending and the ear and eye esteeming and disdaining. As for the beauty of this kindly peak: cave chambers can rest the body, zhi and herbs can fill the hunger, its depths are deep and dim and the dust of the world is far cut off; and with the halls adorned, a host of spirits lodge there. Those who long for it may look but not reach, may come but not stay. Truly it is a real realm before one’s eyes, a Penglai of the human world. Could one but suddenly untie the snares of heaven and sit and shatter one’s fetters, why need one ride a long rainbow and carry feathered wings, or borrow Master Anqi and probe secret arts? This has no merit of building, yet it shares the mountain and sea itself; what use is a record? So I made this inscription, saying:

Heaven and earth first gave birth, and mountains and rivers are the storehouse; a host of spirits return there, the ancestor of all beginnings. High is the mountain, deep is the sea; truly this Great God is a bridge over the ford of suffering. The dark-blue hall towers, white clouds wreathe round, for men to look up to and rely on, the people’s protection. It is all your merit, all your virtue. Let him whose will is to feed on the clouds forever still the workings of dust. Looking up to the vast heavens, looking down to the king of valleys: let these be matched with the Sage’s long life, boundless through a billion ages.
Record of the Repair of Dajue Chan Temple on Ling Mountain

Jimo lies in the east of the three Qi, girt with mountains and belted with the sea, and is called a mighty county. It has Tianzhu on the left and Maling on the right, looks down on Hualou and rests its back on Ling Mountain: a great spectacle indeed. Ling Mountain is thirty li north of the seat of government, and on its summit is Dajue Temple, an ancient monastery of Tang and Song whose origins are lost and cannot be examined. In the Chenghua era of our Ming it was first moved to the mountain’s northern foot, at the elbow of the village’s stem; hence the village’s good fortune rested on it, and with the years the halls daily fell into ruin and the dharma-body lay broken among the weeds. A certain Mr. Zhang and others of the village gathered the clan and took counsel, saying: Dajue is our lookout monastery. I remember its flourishing days, when morning bells and evening chanting woke us from our stupor and urged us to diligence, and our lives depended on it. Now it is silent. Who will be our bridge? Without a great good teacher we cannot raise it ourselves. So with one accord they reverently invited Chan Master Guifeng to preside. The Master’s dharma name was Xingxiang; he came first from a great clan of Pingdu. In youth he bore a rare spirit, and was a man of noble, free bearing. He began by studying the words of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, and looked on life as a floating fragment, but had a mind set beyond the world. Presently he abandoned what he had learned and inquired into the Yellow Emperor and Laozi’s arts of escaping the body, saying: This is still within the furnace and hammer. So he pledged his heart to the Buddhist school and bowed to a certain master of a certain temple in the county. Afterward, sandals on his feet and umbrella on his back, he traveled west to the upper capital, first receiving the tenets of Tiantai and Xianshou from Master Xiao of Shutang, and then studying with Chan Master Xiaoshan Shu of Shaoshi, transmitting Bodhidharma’s mind-seal. He mastered both Chinese and Sanskrit and penetrated the schools of nature and marks, so that for a time the scholars of doctrine all made room for him and straightened their robes. Then he returned east to his old estate and hid there several years. Hearing of this mountain’s invitation, he rose gladly and said: Long ago our Dajue descended at Ling Mountain, and when the Dharma-banner stood the crooked wind fell. My will is here. So staff in hand he came to the temple, opened the weeds and cut the brambles, and day by day made clear to his disciples the work they had undertaken. Within a year his Way-wind greatly revived, and the crooked schools and heterodox ends that came to his gate to be rebuked and corrected cannot be numbered. Dwelling here, the Master toiled ceaselessly at building: giving up his robe and bowl, cutting down food and drink, his lips parched and his stomach emptied, he saved for several years and reckoned a certain sum; then he came out and with Mr. Zhang and the others bought timber and gathered labor, opening forest and breaking ground. In such a year and month the work began and in such a year and month it was completed: halls and corridors, the abbot’s quarters, kitchen and store, the mountain gate, bells and drums, all complete. The flying eaves dazzled the eye and all was radiantly new, the grandest show of the district. In the summer of the guiwei year I hid my name by the sea and visited the Master below Ling Mountain, and he asked me for a record. Let me try to discuss it. The custom of Qi prizes profit and merit and loves boasting and deceit — this has been commonly said since ancient times. Yet its people’s nature is simple and can be taught; hence it is said that one transformation brings it to Lu and a second to the Way. Our Buddhist school came from far India to the eastern summer land and beyond the nine provinces, and the teaching has spread through the world for more than a thousand years. Looking through the records, in the east of Qi there was not a single man. Was the custom of profit and boasting its natural disposition? It was only that no one had guided it well. The Chan Master, inheriting the ills of a hundred generations and rising in a remote corner, with bitter heart and roused will took our Way upon himself and stood alone; within a few years he changed the whole face of things. The Eastern Sea is vast, and it may be called the manner of a Buddha-land: one may say he brought it to the Way in a single transformation, so swift was his influence. Those who dwell in this monastery hereafter, calming the mind in Chan and sitting in stillness, doing morning and evening homage, will pray for our ruler and bless our people, spread the wind of compassion through a billion ages, and light the sun of Buddha in the heavy dark, so that those who see this monastery may awaken the mind through the very matter at hand and change their thoughts at the wind’s breath, unfolding the dark sound where no echo was and opening a broad highway through the thorns. Then the Master’s dharma-body will abide forever in the sound of the stream and the color of the mountains. I was then afflicted with a hidden grief, and moreover the Master and I had walked the field of stillness one after the other; so I have recorded it in full.
Record of the Causes and Conditions of the Sandalwood Tathāgata-Garbha (with Praise)

The wealth of China gathers in the southeast, and its great merchants are called a sea of abundance. In Xinan of She County the Wu family is most prominent, and the layman Kangyu grew up among them. He alone stood out, his will set on the matter above; had he not long practiced prajñā with deep roots, how could he draw a lotus from the mud of desire? The gentleman had long studied under Chan Master Daguan, and so had heard of the Dharma-gate; I had long known him deeply though I had not seen him. In the winter of the yiwei year, as I was going to Leiyang, my road passed through Zhenzhou. The layman welcomed me into his chamber and happened to bring out the sandalwood Tathāgata-garbha, and I bowed in reverence to it. The treasury is made from a single branch of seaside sandalwood five inches high and two inches or so across, split in two and cleft into three, carved with the secret treasury of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas. Its images are more than two hundred, and the Buddha-lands of the ten directions are all contained within. On the half that remains whole, at the lowest half-inch or so, is carved the pool of seven jewels. In the pool, among the lotuses, are cranes, peacocks, parrots, śāri birds, and shared-lifetime birds, shaped like giant ants, filling the spaces among the flowers. Above the pool rises a diamond terrace within the lotuses, with railed galleries in rows, also half an inch or so high. On the terrace is knotted a diamond seat, guarded by two strong men. Then in order three tiers, each tier holding one storey of pavilion: the lower with fourteen bays, the upper with fifteen, each an inch or so high. In the center is set one chief Buddha Vairocana, his body the size of an olive pit, with eleven companion Buddhas surrounding him before and behind, figuring the eight directions and above and below. In the two storeyed pavilions are also set fifteen companion Buddhas each, figuring the two quarters above and below that witness the Dharma. Above this, for the remaining inch and a half or so, all is like empty space, with layered clouds of emptiness, in each row ten Buddhas, thirty in all, figuring this quarter’s chief Buddha-land, the clouds of the three times and ten directions gathering. Its two side pillars, two-tenths of an inch or so wide, are carved vertically with clouds of the ocean of fragrant water, and in the clouds are scattered like stars ten Buddhas, figuring the attendant lands that surround it, each of varying size, like beans, like wheat, all ranged in layers upon layers to display the inexhaustible. This is the whole half. The other half is again divided into two, making two doors: closed they are one, opened they are three, figuring the dhāraṇī; their making is equal to the whole. At the very bottom, like the lotus ocean-assembly, are carved two jeweled boats, each with five great beings seated in it, ten in all, figuring the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds who ferry and save the evil world of the five turbidities. Above this are three tiers of towers, each tier two petals, each with eight Buddhas, forty-eight in all, figuring the great vows. Above this, equal to empty space, are also in each cloud fifteen Buddhas, thirty in all, figuring the companion lands of other quarters, the clouds of the three times and ten directions gathering. Outside the pavilion are the gods and the eight classes holding clouds of incense and flowers, drifting slowly in, each with all kinds of auspicious offerings. On the rim and spokes of the wheel the clouds of palaces are full and arrayed; the miscellaneous beings within and without are jumbled together, thirty-two in all, figuring response according to kind. All these have bodies of varying size, like awns, like wisps; all join their palms facing one another, fully expressing their awe-inspiring power. As for the adornment of the pavilions, so subtle and minute, nothing is lacking, and it cannot be named. In sum, it wraps the ten voids and contains the three times, figuring the secret treasury of the three virtues. Chief and companions layer upon layer, like a crystal bottle holding many mustard seeds: the boundless ocean-assembly blazes forth within a square inch. This is the banner. Below, it is set in the ocean of fragrant water, above the seven-jeweled rim of encircling mountains. The mountains are two inches or so high, inlaid with the seven jewels as adornment; the sea water eddies and swirls, with golden sand spread at the bottom, like fragrant hearts. The two dragon kings Sāgara and Vaiśravaṇa well up from the sea, holding incense and flowers in their hands as offerings, and cover it above with clouds of maṇi jewels, adorned with all kinds of mixed gems. In the clouds is knotted a niche an inch or so high, housing a transformation image of Vairocana with three heads and six arms, seated on a lotus terrace, dignified and at ease, figuring the honored and special. In sum, Buddha-realms layer upon layer, exquisite and wondrously fair: a vast Buddha-land taken into a square inch. All this depicts what can be depicted, and cannot depict what cannot be depicted. I have heard that the spiritual powers of the Buddhas are inconceivable and the karmic actions of beings are inconceivable. Now by inconceivable karmic power this inconceivable Buddha-work is done; and looking at this art of dense and minute carving, there is truly something that cannot be conceived. Those who understand say that without spiritual power such beauty could not be achieved. I say otherwise. What a sage does is always one matter: for the most part he sets up images according to things, and through images reveals the mind. Hence Zaobai’s commentary on the great sūtra sets forth the Dharma through event after event — there is deep meaning in it. To figure the dharma-body by sandalwood is to take the sense of the pure and distant secretly penetrating and entering deeply without interval. Hence it is said: Only one firm and dense body appears in every mote of dust. Truly living beings originally have the dharma-body, but perfumed by the karmic power of ignorance it becomes the illusory body of the five aggregates, so that they do not notice it in daily use, and have long lain sunk in darkness. They do not know that the square inch of awakened mind contains inconceivable Buddha-work. I see that the maker has expressed it by five inches of sandalwood: separated into three, joined into one, and realm upon realm of Buddhas is complete within it. It is precisely to make the viewer store it in mind and picture it with the eye, so that this illusory body and mind of the five aggregates may in a single thought suddenly see the original truth, and the three poisons be perfumed and transformed into the secret treasury of the three virtues, until the Buddha-lands of the ten directions are clear before mind and eye. Alas, if the viewer can by this perfume and cultivate, one day turning freely, seeing the Flower Store before his eyes and the dharma-body at this very moment, then the maker’s spiritual power holds something greatly inconceivable. As for this banner, its origin is unknown; I think it could only have come from a palace treasury. It was long kept in the house of the layman’s nephew. I say it must have come from the Western Regions, from the hand of a master of cunning illusion, or have been brought by Sanskrit masters in Jin or Tang; likely it was lost at the end of Song and drifted among the people of Jiangnan, and so by a chain of conditions has today appeared before the layman. Otherwise, how could it be here? Ah, to know the meaning of Buddha-nature one should observe the time and its conditions. That the layman obtained this — is it not held by the power of the root of kindness? It is no accident. I bowed to it earnestly, leaping with joy again and again; so I have recorded the whole course in detail for the viewer, hoping that through the setting he may illumine his mind and make a diamond seed. Then the layman, trading in the ocean of Buddha-nature, will have turned it into the work of saving beings. If one day he can break a single mote of dust and bring forth the sūtras of a great thousand worlds, he will not only see the maker’s mind but know for himself the wondrous benefit of the merit, which compared with this trifling hair’s tip is greatly inconceivable. Wishing to proclaim its meaning again, I praise it in a verse:

The wondrous dharma-body of all Buddhas has fallen into the five aggregates; its vast and mighty spiritual power turns into the karma of delusive thought, and it drifts on the sea of birth and death, poisoned by suffering without shore. Then there arose a man of great wisdom who skillfully applied the power of means, and from sandalwood fashioned this secret treasury, wherein the boundless realms of all Buddhas are gathered and contained, with every kind of wondrous adornment, inconceivable. I now look on this banner and find the ocean of the Flower Store: it lies only in a single mote of dust yet holds the sūtras of a great thousand worlds. How much more does five inches of incense hold the whole Dharma-realm. Only with the eye of wisdom can one understand this inconceivable work. I gather my thoughts before the pavilion, wishing to see the realms of all Buddhas. By the power of this finger-snap may its gate suddenly open, and I suddenly see within the void the lands of the ten directions filling it. Then I know that between brow and lashes, in the square inch of awakened mind, this rare mark appears — and I do not give rise to thoughts of the marvelous. A great man is brave and bold: amid the five desires he breaks with force the pass of birth and death, like a lotus rising from the water. With the wealth of merit he can build this inconceivable work and set it in the pit of birth and death as a cause for leaving the world. In daily use it stands before one; in light and dark it is never left. Without moving a half-step one visits all good teachers; the boundless ocean of Dharma-gates is gathered in a single mote of dust. May this Dharma-wheel turn on to the end of the future. Those who see, hear, and bow in reverence, who praise and extol it, by a single thought of rejoicing at once complete the supreme seed.

Record of the Pavilion for Contemplating the Precious Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra

Record of Contemplating the Precious Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra: this was written for the sake of contemplating the sūtra. Because this sūtra points directly at living beings’ storehouse consciousness, which is the Tathāgata-garbha, and reveals the states manifest before one in daily use, causing one to observe them in accord and reach the measure of one’s own mind’s manifestation, suddenly realizing all Buddhas’ self-awakened noble wisdom, it is called the Buddha’s word; the mind is not letters, and how can it be understood by letters? Therefore I do not call it a commentary but a record of contemplating the sūtra, taking contemplation as the wandering of the mind and recording the states seen within contemplation. This sūtra was spoken for those who set forth on the supreme vehicle; it is what is called a Dharma most profound and deep, which few can believe. Its text is perilous and its meaning dark: old teachers and long-studied scholars cannot punctuate it when they read it, how much less discard the words and gain the meaning so as to enter the measure of their own mind’s manifestation. Long ago Bodhidharma transmitted it to the Second Patriarch as the mind-seal. Since the Fifth Patriarch taught men to read the Diamond, this sūtra has not only been letters but has been tied up on a high shelf, and few know of it while many gaze at its cliffs. Our Sage Ancestor, with his vast and non-dual true mind, in the leisure of ruling the world and cultivating letters, used the three sūtras of Laṅkāvatāra, Diamond, and Buddha-Ancestors to test monks for ordination, as the Confucians use examinations, and specially commanded the monk Zongle and others to annotate them and promulgate them through the land; but as time went on those who practiced them grew few. In youth I entered the gate of emptiness, my will set earnestly on the matter above, and I was ashamed that I had not passed through many lectures. I once saw the ancients say that the learning of letters cannot penetrate a man’s source of nature; what matters is wondrously awakening to one’s own mind. Once the mind is awakened, then looking back on letters is like pushing a door and having the peg fall into place — it is surely not hard. So I entered the mountains and practiced dry Chan, until I reached the place of not knowing a single character. One day I was suddenly and utterly confident, and looking back on the sūtras they were indeed as clear as the old road home. Only with this sūtra did I suffer from being unable to punctuate it. In the summer of the renchen year of Wanli I dwelt by the sea and happened to suffer unbearably from pain in the foot; so I had this sūtra placed on my desk and quietly bent my strength to it. Suddenly all was still and I forgot my body; and when I opened the scroll and read the hundred and eight meanings, they were as clear as black and white. Then I remembered what the Sanskrit master at Mount Wu had said long before, and so I set down my notes. By the chapter on production and extinction the pain was gone. In the spring of the yiwei year, when I met with trouble for spreading the Dharma, in the midst of confinement a single thought of lone light did not go dark; truly I relied on the awe-inspiring power of this Dharma-gate. Lately I received the grace of banishment to Leiyang. In the spring of the bingshen year, passing through Jizhou, I met the great official Lord Wang Xingxie in the Pure Land, and he asked my help with this sūtra. I brought out the two chapters I had drafted, and he approved; then, with the annotation of true reception and the three translations, he bowed and asked me to finish the work. I carried them with me. On the tenth day of the third month of that year I reached the place of exile, and on the first day of the fourth month I put brush to paper. It was a time of famine and plague, and the dead covered the fields. I sat in the poisonous mist of the charnel ground, daily studying this sūtra, forgetting sleep and food, clear as though in a land of coolness. By the first day of the seventh month I had just finished half the fascicles. With the provincial graduate Ke Fuyuan I led the village elders to bury the corpses, more than four thousand heads, and held an Ullambana assembly, expounding the precepts for the dark ones, aiding them all. Then heaven rained, and the plague stopped with it, causing the land of the barbarians to give rise to great joy. Was this not borrowing one drop from Xingxie to moisten this scorched ground? Afterward I came to Wuyang at the provincial command and rested among the ramparts of the eastern suburb, and began work again on the first day of the tenth month, laying down the brush on the Buddha’s enlightenment day of the following year. I privately think that through many lives, by the condition of slandering the Dharma, I have drawn this recompense; yet by the imperial compassion I was tamed by a journey of ten thousand li, made to enter what is hard to enter, and within a year, though half of it was spent running about, I could finish this vast cause accumulated through kalpas. Had I not relied on the Buddhas’ spiritual power and blessing, how could I with a thinking mind measure the Tathāgata’s self-awakened noble wisdom to such a degree? Therefore I am the more grateful for the imperial grace; to split my bones would hardly repay it. When the draft was done, the provincial judge Lord Zhou of Haimen wished to print it but did not manage it, being called to court to congratulate. In the winter of the wuxu year the censor Lord Fan Youxuan was banished to Leiyang over the matter of establishing an heir and was in the same ranks as I. Passing through Xiancheng he asked what the scenery of Leiyang was like. I laughed and said: It lies in the man, not the setting. And I brought out the draft and showed it to him, saying: This is my Leiyang scenery. He sighed and said: Truly a banner of light. And he wished to spread the Dharma-gift, and so wrote a call for subscriptions to print it. The officials, elders, and lay believers each joyfully completed it. May this excellent cause be turned toward the ocean of the Laṅkāvatāra’s Dharma-nature. Relying above on the perfect illumination of the light of wisdom, may it break this former transgression and quickly ascend to liberation. May those who see and hear and rejoice together enter the measure of their own mind’s manifestation and together turn this Dharma-wheel on to the end of the future. By this merit may I above repay the imperial grace and below raise up the painful destinies, and may all alike ascend the other shore of nirvāṇa. This sūtra single-mindedly breaks the one-sided and crooked views of the outsiders and the two vehicles and causes right wisdom to arise; it takes the one mind as the true doctrine and the crushing of the crooked and revealing of the right as its great function. The clingings it breaks each have their grounds, all recorded in their own schools. In this land of pestilence I bitterly lack sūtras and treatises for reference; even what I cite is all from the Awakening of Faith and Consciousness-Only, to raise the main doctrine, the task being to blend the three translations and make the blood-line run through. As for single-mindedly raising the upward matter and pointing directly at the one mind, washing away all branch words and divergent sayings, and secretly matching the ancestral seal — how dare I yield that to another? Therefore I have set out the course of it thus. Written on the full moon of the last month of summer in the jihai year of Wanli by the monk Deqing of Haiyin.
Stele Record and Inscription of the Huayan Bodhimaṇḍa of the Thousand-Day Long Term Established at Nanhua Temple

Caoxi is the crown of the world’s Chan monasteries; from its one vein the five houses branched, its source like the Zhu and Si rivers. But lying remote beyond the ridges, with the roads closed and barred, lofty men and superior scholars rarely set foot there; and its monks, with narrow sight and hearing, win their rice by farming the fields and no longer know that there is a matter above. This custom has lasted long. Master Daguan and I have always deeply sighed over it, and often had a wish that could not be fulfilled. In the spring of the bingshen year I received the grace of banishment beyond the seas, and took the road to pay reverence to the Sixth Patriarch’s flesh body. Seeing the strictness of its incense and offerings and the extreme decay of the monastery, I could not but weep till my tears wet my robe, and after one meal I left. Before long the governor, the Left Marshal Lord Chen, deeply mindful of the famous mountain’s desolation, wished to settle me there. I knew well that I had brought disgrace on the Dharma-gate and was moreover in the ranks of exiles; how dared I take up affairs? Afterward the provincial judge Lord Zhou of Haimen and Lord Zhu Xingcun both urged it strongly, and I began to turn, though I had not yet had time to settle. In the ninth month of the autumn of the wuxu year the Venerable Jingkong, with the temple monks Xingyu, Zhenquan, Jingtai and others, came to see me at Wuyang; at one sight I was delighted at the sound of his step. The Venerable said: I was born in western Shu, near Emei, and emulated Samantabhadra’s vow-power; so I traveled through every quarter, making the feeding of monks my Buddha-work. Recently I came from north to south and paid reverence to the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi, and I wish, at that excellent bodhimaṇḍa, to form a cause of feeding monks to the number of one hundred and eight thousand, to requite my original vow. I rose gladly and said: How great is the Venerable’s vow-power. Vast it is indeed, but the place where you would give is not yet right. To form a host of conditions one needs the crossroads of the world, where travelers and half-monks pass; but Caoxi lies far beyond the ridges, and the monks in their robes dread the road and rarely reach it. How could one, for the sake of a meal, tread the perils of mountains and rivers? And it is not for food that they come — the Sage’s instruction is in our ears. Dharma-food is equal; Vimalakīrti transmitted the mind. Let the Venerable take the Dharma as guide and food as support: this is what is meant by entering the vinaya through the fragrant rice, the excellent counsel by which our Buddha benefits the world and the wondrous practice cultivated by bodhisattvas. The Venerable heard it gladly and leaped to the work. With Yu, Quan, Tai and the others he strove to manage it, resolving to form a thousand-day long term and assembling forty-eight sincere practicing monks to kneel and recite the great Huayan Sūtra a certain number of times, beginning in the tenth month of that year and ending on the full moon of the tenth month of the xinchou year. At the beginning of the term, when the banner pole was first raised, far and near turned to the wind and the gold grain piled up like clouds; through the six periods they bowed and recited, bells and chanting mingling. Though there was no master on the jeweled seat, the sounds and forms were enough to move the gods and startle the four assemblies. Three years were as one day. Had not the Great Master the Sixth Patriarch shone with the light of quiescent stillness and the mountain spirits guarded it, how could it have come to this? This too is the vanguard of the Dharma-way. The Venerable, glad that his great vow was requited, was about to go far with his staff; and he wished to record on firm stone the names of those who gave and those who received, to make manifest the past and open the future and hand it down undying. I was then engaged in the work of restoration and entered the mountain at the term’s end; seeing them ranged like a forest, I joyfully joined my palms and praised them, saying:

The pure dharma-body: grass and trees, tiles and pebbles; the constant light meets the eye, yet those who see do not know it. The mountain of Baolin has a look of its own; the water of Caoxi has a sharper taste. Before the patriarch came the mountains and waters were already opened; when the patriarch arrived his Way blazed. When the patriarch entered extinction the mountains and waters lay bare; men drink and peck and dwell at peace, not knowing why. Not deaf, not blind, yet like the blind and foolish; gathering firewood and drawing water, they use it all amiss. In the monastery’s late autumn the grass withers and the water dries. I think of taking refuge; I long for it as for water. Though branch and leaf have withered, what passes is like this. I came planting my staff, wishing to dredge it. Then there was the Venerable who followed my wish too, drawing the Flower Store’s stream and first opening a single thread. Grain by grain of rice, like a realm of fragrant food; spoonful by spoonful of water poured into the Flower Store ocean. The bellies of those who eat are measured with the void; the blessing of those who give is blessing beyond end. The Venerable’s will is full; my wish is not yet so. In one mouthful swallowing it all, the patriarch then appears.
Record of the Repair of Hongfu Temple at Pengcheng

The Buddhadharma draws in and gathers many conditions, as though joining separate streams and returning them to the sea. Hence it is said: Of the four seas, the sea is the ultimate; and the Yellow River is one of the four rivers, pouring east from Kunlun, and so the True Land began. When the flood rose to heaven there was the divine Yu, who hewed the Dragon Gate, opened the nine channels, and guided the hundred streams down to Xu; he opened Lüliang and drew the many branches and returned them to the sea.
