What passes is like this: the merit of order has been one vein through all ages. Our Dharma’s coming from west to east is just the same. I observe that in China the famous mountains and great monasteries, the jeweled palaces and Brahma halls, and whatever keeps the Dharma-vein flowing in an unbroken source — their founding merit is not merely that of a divine Yu. Moreover what Yu governed was not the water of nature but the traces of the conditioned; and he still wore out his shins and peeled his skin, and passed his own gate three times without entering, and only succeeded after bitter toil and wasting. Now we must hew the hard obstruction of ignorance, dredge the great flood of the Dharma-nature, tread the conditions of difference, and gather them home to the ocean of enlightenment — how is this easy? Without equal mind and a vow unto death it is assuredly hard. Pengcheng lies at the vital point of the Yellow River; the sky-poured torrent, pouring from a roof-tile height, reaches here at its extreme. Who can withstand its racing rush? Hence its harm is not shallow; even with a divine Yu, what could one do? The layman Su Dongpo once governed this prefecture, and cherishing an age-old anxiety he built the Yellow Tower to press it down — yellow being earth — taking the sense of subduing and governing. North of the city he built Huangfu Temple to pillow on the flood and lodge the Chan practice. But the layman saw deeply into the source of nature and marks, taking the sense of mutual merging: when merged they do not overpower one another, and the rushing water flows in peace, and it will be an eternal blessing to the living people of the land. Hence those who transmit it today also call it Hongfu, Great Blessing; its meaning is subtle. The temple has now been washed and battered by the river water; must it not be that one who wondrously understands the true emptiness of the water of nature should preside? Chan Master Daguan Ke, traveling north, often rested his staff here and deeply sighed over it. So he greatly opened a Dharma society and charged the ācārya Lord Ci of Cifeng to hold the precepts of nature with refinement; and he wrote a call to gather many conditions, and to renew it in a universal assembly. He would cause those who go to pass and those who come to rest, each alike entering the ocean of Dharma-nature, and so guide the one vein that came from the west, in the hope of an eternal blessing for the beings of the great earth. How like a divine Yu was the Master’s mind; truly it was bitter toil. The great officials and lay believers all at once brought forth the supreme cause of the Way. This is like the three gates already opened and the seven wells already dug, a pillar in midstream standing firm against the fallen waves, while for a thousand li the water flows in peace, boats come and go with the wind, ships pass up and down; then the merit of drawing and gathering is easy enough. Lord Ci travels by sledge over the land; he must not grudge his shins, but with equal mind and a vow unto death put forth his strength and plan early, not letting the months slip by. Yet to plan the hard through the easy and do the great through the small: I have said that a drop of water entering the sea dries up together with the Bohai; but if one does not refuse the small streams, they gradually become deep and broad. With this as vanguard, a weight of ten thousand jun is easily lifted. On another day, when the towers and halls are adorned like the Jetavana monastery, I shall with a broad long tongue pour out an endless stream and reckon the blessing of gods and men of this assembly.

On the tenth day of the summer solstice in the yiwei year of Wanli I met with trouble for spreading the Dharma and was sentenced to exile at the ridges and seas. The Great Master Da, with blistered feet, traveled several thousand li north to console me, and we agreed to meet here. When I arrived, the Master had already bought a boat and gone south. The host brought out his call to subscription; reading it I felt a long, vague sigh, and so by candlelight I wrote this at random with my brush, to form a bond for another day. The words may seem out of order; it is only that one who has often been a traveler pities the traveler the more.
Record of the Founding of the Long Life Hermitage

Three li or so west of the city of Guangdong is a place called the Small Garden, backed by hills and belted by the sea, a deep recess of monasteries. Its ground has long stored numinous beauty. In the gengchen year of Wanli a Chan monk named Rushou came from Chu and spread his teaching here; for a time rich merchants and great traders, and townsmen of note and conduct, mostly took refuge with him. All wished to invite him as their chanting guide, and each spread gold to build a monastery as a place for expounding the Dharma. They bought land from a local man of the Pan family, contributed wealth, and gathered workmen, and it was done in no time, named the Long Life Hermitage. Halls above and below, abbot’s quarters on both wings, refectory and kitchen and meditation rooms, beams and rafters joined, the red paint gleaming; and images of the Tathāgata and the great beings were cast, with incense, flowers, bells, and chimes, drums and music and adornments, nothing lacking. Barbarian sounds and Brahma chanting mingled day and night: truly a Jetavana welling up from the earth, an excellent bodhimaṇḍa. When Rushou passed away his disciple Xingliang continued. In the gengyin year Liang again extended the ground and its bounds, and gate and walls were radiantly new. In the spring of the bingshen year I was graciously banished to Leiyang and passed by this hermitage, staying two nights before I left. The next year, in the summer of the dingyou year, I left Wuyang at the provincial command, and Liang led the benefactors and disciples, bowed his head, and asked me to record the matter. I gladly gathered my robe and took the seat, waved my whisk, and addressed them all, saying: Buddha-sons, good indeed; listen closely. In mountains and rivers and the great earth there is no place that is not a bodhimaṇḍa; among the scaled, shelled, feathered, and furred there is no creature that is not Buddha-nature. How much more this land of Guangdong, the grandest beauty between the two worlds, and these humans, the most numinous of all beings: how could they not at once manifest the Pure Land and see the dharma-body? I remember how the World-Honored One, walking in order with Indra, once pointed to a place and said: Here a monastery should be built; it is where I long ago spread my hair and covered the mud for Dīpaṃkara. Then the elder at once took up a blade of grass and planted it, saying: The monastery is built. And the gods praised him. Buddha-sons, seen thus, wherever one walks is the Tathāgata’s causal ground, and whatever one does is building a bodhimaṇḍa — how much more when one drips fat and draws marrow, sweats blood on muddy roads, to make towers and halls and adornment? It rests entirely on what the giver and receiver are. If the giver does not cling to marks, his merit is like space, measureless and boundless, and the fruit is inconceivable; then a bundle of grass or a drop of water, a grain of rice or a stalk of greens, is equal to the whole Dharma-nature and the void. Otherwise, reckoning merit and calculating profit, though one give seven jewels filling the sands of the Ganges it only adds to the burden of conditioned karma — how then could it win the supreme field of blessing and become a bodhi seed? If the receiver does not stick to traces, then mind-only is the Pure Land and self-nature is Amitābha, and whatever meets the eye is nothing but the Land of Bliss; then a high cliff or deep valley, beneath a tree or among graves, is equal to the land of eternal quiescent light. Otherwise, borrowing a self to steal ease, though one dwell in the Tusita heaven or the Brahma heaven, one only adds to the karmic fruit of birth and death — how then could one benefit self and others and open the eye of gods and men? Buddha-sons, if giver and receiver can forget conditions and leave marks behind, then mind and setting are both empty, the merit done is like space, and the fruit protected is like space. Thus this hermitage, though small, can contain the Dharma-realm and embrace the void: morning bells and evening chanting, moon in water and wind in pines, all proclaim the endless Dharma-sound, to pray for the boundless long life of our Sage Son of Heaven and to nourish the endless blessing of the people. Extend it over the whole earth and there is no place that is not a happy land; spread it to the ten directions and there is no man who does not realize the truth. Then the hermitage is the field of bliss and man is Measureless Life. Thus naming it Long Life is fitting. Otherwise, water, soil, wood, and stone are the four marks of the conditioned, changing and flowing on, no more than a heat-haze or a flower in the air — what long life is there? The great assembly, hearing these words, rejoiced, bowed, and withdrew. So I wrote this.
Record of the Repair of Tianxin Temple on Yao Mountain in Yingde County (with Inscription)

The ridges lie remote in the southeast, bordering the various Qiang; in Zhou and Qin they did not pay tribute or submit. Yet today they are not only a land of letters and elegant culture, spreading through China, but their jeweled palaces and Brahma halls are mighty in every place. From the Liang dynasty, when Bodhidharma crossed the sea and came from India, and in the Tang the Sixth Patriarch, whose robe and bowl were renowned at Caoxi, the Chan grove’s teaching became the school of the eastern land. How could heaven and earth limit its Way, or mountains and rivers keep its qi to themselves? Truly it lies in finding the right man to spread it and doing it at the right time. Yingde in Shao is a foot from Caoxi; a hundred li or so west of the prefectural seat is Tianxin Temple on Yao Mountain, which too was founded in an earlier age — was it a descendant of Caoxi? It is lost and cannot be examined. When the present emperor took up the great rites of the Eastern Palace there was first an order to gather pearls, and the eunuch Lord Li of the Imperial Horse Pasture, a close attendant of the Qianqing Palace, was specially sent to Ao to supervise the work. In the seventh month of the autumn of the wuxu year of Wanli he came to Qingying; before long, because of the fire in the two palaces and three halls, great works were under way, the armies east and west were raised, and the treasury was reported empty, an order to open mines was again issued, all entrusted to the Lord. He received the command with utmost care, going to sea against wind and wave and climbing mountains in the face of tigers and wild oxen, serving those above and nurturing those below with a heart of loyalty and love, quiet and without disturbance; and the people of the land received his kindness in good measure. In the autumn of the jihai year his circuit came to Yingde, and searching deep into the mines he passed by a ruined temple. The Lord was grieved and said to the elders: The spirits are the numinosity of mountains and rivers, the masters of misfortune and blessing; how much more is the Buddha, the Sage, honored by the world, and a monastery the people’s field of blessing. How can it lie waste like this? So he donated a sum from his granary funds, and gave a call to the good people of the place to gather strength and finish the work. Before long the conditions gathered, workmen were assembled and timber cut; the work began in the winter of that year and was completed in the autumn of the xinchou year. Wind and sound answered; a hundred strengths came together; halls and corridors, the mountain gate and monks’ quarters, were radiantly new. The Lord asked me for a writing to carve on firm stone and hand down undying. Moved by the Lord’s virtuous intent and his kindness to the people, I made an inscription, saying:

Heaven and earth plant the numinous; mountains and rivers hold excellence. Ghosts and spirits come to dwell there; misfortune and blessing have no excess. Great is Maitreya, honored as the Two-Footed One. All that have teeth or wear hair each receive their true nature. Vast is the teaching’s influence, moving like clouds to the eight bounds; those who have awareness take refuge as grass bends before the wind. Look to the east of the ridges, to the south of Shao, the land of Yingde: its heart is heaven, and heaven’s emperor is who? Great is the Great Enlightened One, chief of Śakra and Brahmā, the bell of the golden mouth. Jeweled palaces and Pure Lands are in every place; the wilds of Cangwu he indeed built. The years shift and alter; wind beats and rain erodes. All that has form is transformed, how much more this rotting growth. The teaching of images decays day by day; who shall guide the deluded path? It is only our Lord, who holds heaven’s tally. Mountain spirits and sea gods leap and run in joy. Passing this far wilderness he gave sincere heart and spread gold; one red banner raised, the response came like an echo. Wondrous and fair the adornment, the ground level as a palm. Gods revere and ghosts submit; gods and men gather everywhere. Blessing covers sands of the Ganges; merit surpasses a hundred billion. Bell sounds and Brahma chanting pray morning and evening for blessing. May our emperor’s life equal heaven and earth. May the Lord’s merit endure with the mountains and rivers; swearing alliance by belt and whetstone, all raise their hands to the brow.
Stele Record of the Temple of Loyalty and Valor (with Inscription)

Guangdong lies at the ridges; its mountains and seas have long bred bandits. Great villains and cunning rogues would seize the high peaks and steep ridges, the long waves and vast waters, winding about like a belt and collar, with the islands ranged like stars, trusting them as walls of metal and a storehouse of heaven. This has been so from of old. Not to speak of the Japanese invading within, these men themselves rampaged, rising one on the heels of another: Wu Ping and Zeng Yiben raged in the Jiajing and Longqing eras, sweeping the seas, with yellow banners and red clothes, usurping the title of Jinghai, wearying our royal armies so that spear and shield knew no rest the year round, while the common people by the sea died until the marshes seemed scorched. When Yiben was taken, his remaining party, such as Zheng Dahan, Lin Daogan, Zhu Liangbao, Xu Junmei, Lin Feng, and Honglao, each split off a corner like bees and spread poison the more. At that time a man of Yue named Wu Tianshang had first made a name among the students but failed repeatedly in the examinations; so he abandoned the scholar’s trade, became a clerk, and by the board’s summons served as secretary to the governor. Lord Sima Yin recognized his ability and brought him in as military adviser, and from time to time consulted him on the lairs and troops of the bandits, and every plan he offered left nothing to chance. Lord Sima marveled greatly at him and strongly recommended him to the Son of Heaven; seven memorials in all before it was approved. The board proposed to raise Shang from the ranks and appoint him General of Pacification, in command of the military affairs of the White Dove Stockade; and the General’s father, sons, and brothers all served in the army. Earlier, by the General’s plan, great red banners were set up along the whole sea coast from Fujian and Guangdong, with strict defenses and laid schemes; and beneath the Grand General, from the officers down to the soldiers, all knew the General’s ability and none failed to follow his intent. Thus the bandits were taken day by day. Only Daogan escaped in a great ship to Siam; the General’s son Rushi followed on his track but did not catch him. Those left were Zheng Dahan, holding Liudu Cove, and Honglao, holding the Pearl Pool, not yet reduced. So Shi was given a thousand troops to surprise Honglao, and he cut down Lao and more than three hundred of his party. Zheng Dahan was met by the General and his younger brother Tianxiang with their own strength. Dahan was a man of Guangdong, huge and wondrous, eight feet tall, his courage the crown of all the bandits; his soldiers were all picked and fierce, and in every battle none dared face his edge. The General had two thousand pacified people who had never known arms. The armies met at Du Cove; Tianxiang, seizing his courage, was first to mount the wall and broke into the ranks, and fighting with all his strength he died. The General, raging, gave one shout and drummed his men on; and so Dahan was taken and his remnant scattered. From that time the wounds of the sea began to heal and the common people could at last eat in peace. Lord Sima marveled greatly at the General’s merit and grieved for Xiang’s death, and reported it fully to the Son of Heaven. The emperor praised it and sent it down to the Grand Marshal to record the merit and reward the service. At that time the people of Du Cove, moved that Xiang had exchanged his life for theirs, raised a temple and sacrificed to him at the seasons, naming it Loyalty and Valor. Lately, when the Japanese slaves violated the eastern border, war continued several years, and the General’s son Shi was still military adviser to the governor of the Two Guangs. By Lord Sima’s command he went to Japan to spy, and the Regent did indeed die; Shi brought back the firearms lost at Biti. The officers marveled at him; before he could report, the Japanese in Korea had already withdrawn. Afterward Lord Sima let the matter rest, and assigned the Guangdong sea troops to Shi to guard against the Japanese slaves and roving bandits, and Liudu happened to be his station. Shi, moved by past events and grieving for his uncle Xiang’s death while the grass-blood was not yet dry and the banners still seemed before his eyes, could not but feel his hair lift his cap. At the outset of his duties he came to me and begged a word to record the matter. I had heard the whole story from the local people, and so, honoring Shi’s merit and emboldened by Xiang’s death, I made an inscription, saying:

Great and glorious Heaven, blessing the good and punishing the lewd: those cunning villains — why were they born? Once the cunning are born they are long snakes and great swine, sucking brains and drinking fat, and the day knows no rest. In the blaze of the imperial awe the host is marshaled. Stalwart tiger generals count the siege mounds a shame. The hunted beast flees to the wood; the fierce tiger rushes out. Driving the market folk to battle, Xiang was first to mount. Tiger against tiger, their strength was matched; teeth sharp and claws keen, the bald one was first wounded. The bald one wounded, his keenness too was broken. Stink endures, fragrance flows; in death they are different. The fragrance flows the more, the glory lasts the longer. The temple image seems alive; boys run and women hasten. Boys run and women hasten; the living spirit grows more numinous. At the seasonal feasts they pour mountains of food and seas of wine, drinking and pecking. Through a thousand autumns and ten thousand years their blessing has no shore.
Record of the Huacheng Hermitage at Kuteng Ridge in Dianbai

In the second month of the spring of the bingshen year of Wanli I was on my way to Leiyang and passed through Dianbai. Twenty-five li or so to the west there is Kuteng Ridge, where I saw men under thatch giving tea to form karmic bonds. Coming newly into the land of pestilence, with the scorching heat poisoning a man, my heart oppressed and my strength spent, I was glad at the sight of a ford and bridge, as happy as if entering a phantom city. So I loosened my robe and sat at ease, and after a sound sleep I rose and asked the reason for it. It was the good man Yi Zhentan who, with a dozen or so other good men, had set it up together, because this place is the back gate of Luopang: in former unsettled days bandits came and went and the roads were blocked, and though now it is at peace it is still a feared road. Moreover it lies at the throat between Qiong and Lei, and travelers go in fear; below there is a hot spring rolling and boiling, and to walk there is like treading a cauldron. So they used tea to comfort those who came and went; it was not for expounding the Dharma. And they said it was intended for three years. I admonished them, saying: Beware of doing an inconceivable work with a limited mind. One day a monastery shall be built here as a place of eternal coolness. In the eighth month of autumn I was ordered back to Wuyang by the governor’s office. Two years later, in the wuxu year, the tea-giving term ended. Two of the workers came to see me among the ramparts, and I gave them full ordination and sent them back to their place. Then I wrote a call and had Zhentan and the others collect funds for the building. Within two years it was done, named the Phantom City, taking the sense of pressing on to the jewel place and halting midway to rest from utter weariness. This year, the gengxu year, Zhentan is seventy; his children’s marriages are finished, and he came to pay reverence at Caoxi, asking to be shaved and become a Buddha-son. I gladly shaved and dyed him, giving him the dharma name Fucheng, taking the sense of Sudhana’s southern inquiry, his visits to good teachers being the starting point. For in the land of the barbarians it is not easy to find a man who in his declining years can put on the black robe; his root of faith is rare. This bodhimaṇḍa began and ended with Zhentan alone; and I sent him back to the hermitage to devote himself to the pure karma, bowing and reciting through the six periods. This is the one blade of grass I have planted since coming south, the one dhūta I have saved, hoping to pass the lamp of wisdom in the hot regions and sprinkle sweet dew on the land of pestilence, to be a ford and bridge over the sea of suffering and to moisten the parched flames of the burning house, spreading benefit without end. Therefore I have set out its whole course to hang on firm stone, hoping it may not decay.
Record of the Udumbara Flower at Faxing Temple (with Inscription)

In the jihai year of Wanli, on the first day of the second month of spring, the fourth year of my exile in Guangdong — earlier I had finished the exposition of the Laṅkāvatāra, and for the disciples beneath the bodhi tree I had expounded the Lotus, the Śūraṅgama, and the Consciousness-Only sūtras and treatises, one round of each; black-robed and white-robed inclined their hearts and all at once turned to the wind. At that time the abbot of Faxing Temple invited the scholar Ou Boyu as instructor of the novices, and with full ceremony I presided over this Way and from time to time stirred them up. So a Dharma assembly was established in the Dark Mystery Hall of the Vairocana Hall. Two days before the assembly opened I happened to arrive, and my disciple Tongtong told me: In the courtyard a golden lotus has welled up; pray come and see it, Master. I saw it and rejoiced, saying: Of this I have heard once, and now seen twice. It is a response of the Dharma-way. The flower grows from a banana stem, sending up a stalk and standing straight from it, like a lotus, its color like gold; its leaves are twice as thick and firm, petal upon petal in clusters, enfolding a fragrant heart, shaped like a jade hairpin, hollow within and clean of body, holding sweet dew; draw it up and drink, and the fragrance fills the lungs. It is what the world rarely sees, like what the Buddha called the udumbara flower, which is explained as an auspicious response — is this not its meaning? The sūtra says: The Buddha appears in the world as the udumbara flower, which blooms but once in an age. It is just like the qilin, the phoenix, and the magic fungus born in a prosperous age. Long ago in the Yao and Qin period a twinned flower grew in the palace court, and the divination said that a sage would come from the west. So they sought out Dao’an of Xiangyang, and An recommended Kumārajīva; and Chang raised a hundred thousand armored troops with Lü Guang as grand general, and attacked Kucha to seek Shi. When Shi arrived, the Buddhadharma of Qin flourished from that time. The twinned flower is what is commonly called the double-headed lotus. I remember that in my childhood, when I first left home, my ancestor the Great Master Xilin invited my late master Shouyu to dwell in the stūpa court of Master Zang. Three years before, a golden lotus had suddenly welled up in the court, growing from a banana stem, and those who came to see it numbered a million fingers a day; those who understood said it was an omen of the Dharma-way. Before long my late master was welcomed to dwell in that court, and the flourishing of the Dharma-way in Jiangnan did indeed begin from that. My Dharma elder Xuelang is to this day renowned through the world, no unworthy successor to Kuiji of Cien. This is the first time I have heard of this flower and found it verified. And when I was twenty-five and lay ill three months, I had earlier planted a banana tree with my own hands before the court; its leaves spread wide and it stood more than ten feet, and from it there drew forth a golden lotus, larger by twice than what I see now. Every dawn it received sweet dew enough to fill a cup, and drinking it cooled my five viscera; thus for three months it did not wither, and my illness was finally cured. The elders all said it was just like the stūpa court of Master Zang. I privately rejoiced, saying: Is this not a portent of the Buddhadharma? In the winter of that year I left home and went wandering far, and so to this day. And now I see this flower a second time — is it without meaning? Moreover the qilin, the phoenix, and the magic fungus are the essence of transformation and the upright qi of heaven and earth; concentrated in things they are auspicious responses, and in men they are the favorable appearance of living beings. Hence the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is like the udumbara flower. Confucius said: The phoenix does not come, the river gives forth no diagram; it is over for me. Seen thus, an omen does not respond in vain, and a response must have its cause. In the past, when the Chan vein flowed east, in this Guangdong Guṇabhadra established the diamond at Faxing, and Zhiyao planted the bodhi at the precept platform, saying: In a hundred and sixty years a sage will appear. And when Bodhidharma first came to Wuyang, and Patriarch Lu showed his point in the wind and banner, and Baolin opened its grave, and Caoxi spread its branches, their light shone on sun and moon and their Way covered the world; yet this place has been silent for nearly a thousand years. Is it not that when the branches are great the root is stripped? The patriarch said: The leaf falls and returns to the root; when it comes there is no mouth. Sentient beings come and plant the seed; in the causal ground the fruit is born again. Alas, the udumbara appears again; the sun of Buddha shines afresh; Caoxi, dried up, rises again; the enlightenment flower, withered, blooms once more. For this we look to the present day. So I record its whole course, and make this inscription, saying:

Bright is the auspicious star; glowing the felicitous cloud. I look toward that man of the ultimate; my heart is not at rest. The phoenix is in the suburb; the qilin is in the wild. Far off is the man of the ultimate; how shall my longing cease? That udumbara flower is the omen of the lotus; it wells up and appears from the void — how can it be without meaning? The gold of Jambudvīpa is the color of its bloom; the sweet dew’s juice tastes like this. Twinned in the court, armored hosts on the border: the man of the ultimate indeed comes, and this Way is greatly displayed. Crossing the sea and over the desert, here he plants his banner. Who pulled it up? The huntsman’s company. The banner is pulled up; the going is at its extreme. Nothing goes that does not return; the udumbara has come forth. The udumbara comes forth again, in the lowly and the high. In my life I have seen it three times; how can this Way end?
Record of the Repair of the Pure Land Temple on Nan Mountain in Longchuan County

Among the famous mountains of southern Yue there are many fields of blessing. Their source comes down from Mount Heng, crosses the Yu Ridge, reaches the Shao stones and knits into Caoxi, opening the one vein of the Chan source. A thousand li east, passing the provincial city and coming out at Luofu, immortal traces and sage-like prospects make a grand beauty. Several hundred li further east, at the middle of Chao and Hui, lies Longchuan, the old Xunzhou. Its seat of government commands the upper reaches of Hui and lies at the crossroads of Ou and Yue; its land borders Qian and Zhang, with high mountains and steep ridges where Zhuang and Yao dwell mixed together; formerly there were many bandit lairs, and the people were fierce and hard to govern. Those who came to this land of old despised it as a wayside inn, sitting in the poisonous mist of pestilence, sad and dizzy, with no leisure even to govern themselves — how much less to order ritual and righteousness and raise up teaching and transformation? Its customs: from the time Zhao Tuo of Han returned to benevolence they first knew there was a ruler; in the Tang, when Lord Han sacrificed to the crocodile, they first knew there was culture; and its transformation began when the Sixth Patriarch passed on the robe and Dadian shook his staff, and they first knew there was a Buddha. Thus one knows that heaven and earth have their constant warp, but transformation has no fixed measure. Mountains and rivers await their man as the body awaits the mind: when the mind is true the body is transformed, and where the man is outstanding the land is numinous — truly there is reason in it. The mountains and rivers of Xun are as of old, and our people’s customs are those of former men; in past times it was known for its exiled guests, and one never heard of it being roused by a magistrate’s governance. Now Lord Sun has governed this county, and within three years transformation was accomplished: he polished the people with righteousness, guided the benighted by degrees, and adapted affairs by expedience. He set aside school land, built the Plum Pavilion, made bridges, and built the new city wall, all by donating his own salary and grain. As for repairing the Buddhist temple on Nan Mountain, it was all done with the hairpins, earrings, and dowry of his late wife, wholly given up to make adornment, to assist the Pure Land and cultivate hidden merit. All this is to teach by the way of the spirits, to reveal the mind through the matter at hand, to be a compassionate ship on the sea of suffering and a lamp of wisdom in the long night. The mountain faces the county on the south, its peaks towering and encircled by the great river, its mountains and rivers wondrous, its groves dense. The temple began in the Tang, and was likely founded in the days when Chan Master Dadian’s Dharma flourished. Later its old site became the Shrine of the Two Worthies, to sacrifice to the Song vice-minister Su Zhe and the remonstrating counselor Chen Cisheng; afterward a man of the Luo family seized it as a grave site. In the jihai year of Jiajing the education commissioner Lord Wu restored the shrine, adding the Song chancellor Lord Wu Qian, and sacrificed to them as the Three Worthies; and the temple’s name nearly vanished. In his leisure from government the Lord often went out among them, gazing about and looking up and down, and had long sighed over it. When his wife died in the official residence, at the parting her spirit was calm and still, and she passed away upright, mindful of the Buddha, a person of the lotus pool. The Lord was moved, and poured out her dowry to renew the temple. He separated the shrine into three bays of hall and made images of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the lotus-pool ocean-assembly and of the eight classes and gods, arrayed like clouds, adorned and wondrously fair, their light blazing — truly the real realm of the Pure Land. To left and right are ranged refectory, kitchen, and meditation rooms, nothing lacking. He invited a certain monk as abbot, with morning and evening homage and the mingled sound of bell and chanting. Thus the Western Pure Land stands before one’s eyes, and the spirit’s rebirth does not depart from where one is. It is said: The setting changes with the mind, and the land is numinous through its man, because the great mountains and rivers do not go outside this mind. Seen thus, the Lord’s mind is lifted high above the mountains and rivers, and his wife’s spirit dwells forever in the Pure Land. Above he prays for the realm’s blessing, below for the people’s welfare; the Lord’s merit will be handed down without end — how could it be only the trifling benefit of a field of blessing? The work began in such a year and month and was completed in such a year and month. It was formerly called Nan Mountain and is now named Pure Land, recording its original cause. The Lord’s surname is Sun, his name Yunyi, his courtesy name Tunan; he is a man of Jinsha. He who recorded it is the monk Deqing of Changgan in Baixia.
Record of the Society on Xiuliang Mountain

Long ago when I was on pilgrimage I passed with Master Miaofeng through the waste of Pingyang and lodged on the sunny side of Mount Huo. Far off we saw the crowding peaks, dark green, rising fair above the Milky Way, with misty groves dense; and I thought there must be a holy bodhimaṇḍa there. The Master said: This is Xiuliang Mountain. Long ago a man of the Way ate cypress leaves here, and so it was named. Afterward a monastery was built, called Ciyun. I did not get to climb and view it, but passed by. I dwelt at Mount Wu and went beyond the ridges to the Eastern Sea; and now thirty-seven years have passed, yet it is ever vaguely before my mind and eye. In the spring of the renzi year Chan Master Kongyin of the Qingliang Bamboo Grove sent his disciple Wuci with a letter to inquire after me in the land of pestilence. Asking after the prosperity of the Master’s Dharma-way, he said that the disciples who had long received the benefit of the Dharma had each scattered to hidden dwelling and chosen famous places to nourish their conditions of the Way; and he brought out the Master’s covenant for the society on Xiuliang Mountain, with the preface by the court historian Li Benning. Reading it I sighed deeply and said: Alas, the beauty of mountains and rivers awaits its man to flourish; if the man is not there the Way does not walk in vain — is this not so? I think of how Śākyā descended in spirit at Kapilavastu, and the true and heroic men of the arhats gathered on Vulture Peak, and by causes and conditions sang the Way; Jetavana and the Cock Garden are all traces of responding and transforming according to conditions. This is how Dharma societies began. As the Dharma spread east, every famous mountain in the realm became a place for singing the Way; and from ancient times no man of the ultimate has ever failed, by occupying a fair prospect and lodging in numinous beauty, to hand down the transformation of the Dharma forever. The National Master Guan of Qingliang first expounded the Huayan at Mount Wu, and his Way covered the world, and he was the court master of seven Tang emperors. Since then a thousand years have been silent. Now Master Kong has reopened the Bamboo Grove and greatly spread the teaching of the perfect and sudden; the ten directions gather like clouds and a million fingers surround him — is this not the flourishing of an age? Now his disciples can take embodying the Way as their aim, their will set on hidden dwelling, their minds set on pure karma, tracing the old affair of the cypress-eater and spreading the rain of Dharma at Ciyun. They gather the excellent among black-robed and white-robed, open the gate of non-duality, and establish a society of equality: through the six periods the lotus clepsydra, in one thought refined cultivation; by day they lecture to make clear the doctrine, by night they calm the mind in Chan to still the thoughts. In precepts they follow Upāli, in practice they accord with prajñā; and at once the trees on the cliffs and the sedge in the court, the gibbons’ cry and the cranes’ call, all stand forth as the dharma-body and proclaim the wondrous meaning. What was a dark, silent, utterly lonely place is now radiant as a ground that illumines past and present. Is it not that the mountain spirits awaited their man, and the Way goes with the times, because causes and conditions met? Or is the mind that ate cypress leaves not extinguished today? Because I once passed that place and viewed its fair prospects, and now dwell in the land of pestilence and hear of this undertaking from afar, my mind-ground is cool and I picture their excellent gathering. So I briefly record the outline of its decline and revival, to form a bond for another age. As for the rules of what they establish, the master there has his own covenant and law.
Record of the Repair of Haihui Hermitage (with Inscription)

Lingnan borders on Chu; Caoxi looks toward Nanyue, a thousand li away, and all between is high mountains and steep ridges, with winding, dense hills, and everywhere fine mountains and waters. From the time the Great Master the Sixth Patriarch shook the ridges with his Way, and his disciple Master Rang opened the teaching at Nanyue, from then on the dwelling places of famous monks and great virtuous ones have been found in every spot. Wherever one dwelt alone, in time it became a jeweled monastery and field of blessing, a lookout for its region, in every place. Yizhang lies between the two mountains, near the Shao stones and under Hengyang, and is the necessary road for coming and going. Five li or so from the seat of government there is a mountain called Houpei, its peaks wondrous and fair, its groves dense: truly an excellent bodhimaṇḍa. Lately it was the estate of a local man, Mr. Li, who gave it up as a hermitage and invited Zhenrun, a disciple of Dayong, to dwell there as a place of rest for the lofty wanderers of the ten directions; he named it Haihui. The repair began in the jimao year of Wanli and has come to the guimao year; again it has been worn by wind and rain, and Run’s disciple Ruyao renewed it. Above are the Buddha hall and mountain gate, three bays each; to left and right the abbot’s quarters and refectory and kitchen, all complete. There are a hundred mu of land yielding two bushels of tax grain, and its cultivation can support more than ten men; so wanderers coming and going may have one meal and one night without seeking outside. This too is a phantom city. I have dwelt beyond the ridges eight years, and the authorities invited me into Caoxi to do the sweeping for the Great Master the Sixth Patriarch. The hermitage monk Ruyao came to see me and asked for a record; so I have plainly recorded the matter, and make this inscription, saying:

Lo, Nanyue settles Jing and Xiang; it puts forth branch and trunk and spreads to the far wilds. Winding a thousand li, the Yu Ridge coils high; Baolin stands in their midst, and the water of Caoxi is cold. The water of Caoxi takes its source in India; then there was a man of the ultimate who bathed these Way-bones. The Way-bones seem alive; the water flows unceasing, scattered into sweet dew, becoming rain and marsh. On the sunny side of Yizhang, at the foot of Houpei, a phantom city wells up for the people’s blessing. The phantom city is not far; the jewel place is near, to receive the weary and give them rest, that all may come and take refuge. Taking refuge in our Master, they may bow to his true likeness. May this ground be preserved, with blessing without end.
Record of the Jilong Hermitage at Shuixi in Nanxiong

From Mount Heng the Yu Ridge lifts its trunk, runs east and comes down to Nanpu, commanding river and lake and receiving homage from the north; its rushing waters race away on the opposite course, entering the great prefecture of Nanhai. It holds the upper reaches and gathers all Yue, seizes its throat, and screens the central plain: truly the metropolis of the southeast, pouring from a roof-tile height and overseeing the hundred streams — such is its importance. The prefectural city backs on the ridge and fronts the river, with the two rivers embracing it, standing grand and imposing, looking toward the great sea like a shield in the void. One who goes upstream is as though climbing to heaven and touching the clouds, visible but unreachable. Here the mountains fly and the waters run, resting and gathering nowhere, so the principle of life is not retained; hence the people live in haste, chasing profit as they chase the waves, and those who are well-off and have stores laid by against the unexpected of the year are few. Thus heaven and earth, mountains and rivers, are like the four seasons, never all at once, and hard to keep whole and firm; they must rely on men to shape them. Therefore the saying about mending heaven is no falsehood. Looking at those who governed this prefecture of old, any with the least Dharma-eye could not escape the anxiety of one who strains his sight; and if he had the will to pull back the fallen waves and dam the hundred streams, he must borrow human strength to mend it. All who had business here must build temples, raise stūpas, and set bells and drums to meet it; and often the success came like an echo, while men never knew why. Let me try to explain. Among things, the numinous one whose transformations cannot be measured is the dragon; hence the ruler is figured by it. The sage is like the dragon: clouds move and rain falls, and the ten thousand things take their life from it. As for the talk of geomancers, the nine schools do not count it worth mentioning; and yet they say that if one seeks the dragon and needles its point, success blazes like a kindled fire — why? For when the needle finds the vessel, it commands the work of raising the dead; as when a man’s illness lies in the vital region, and food and drink cannot reach it, one must reach it with needle and moxa. Thus to cut off the wind-dragon and inject the earth-vein one must build temples, raise stūpas, and set bells and drums, just as one treats the vital region with needle and moxa. Moreover heaven and earth are one body and yin and yang one qi; the mountains are the bones and the rivers the vessels. The dragon’s virtue is to hide, and its nature flames beyond control. Those who reared dragons of old must have had an art; with that art in hand, at a shadow they submit. Every art that is numinous must be of the utmost essence; those who do not know think it marvel and wonder. Yet what a thing loves it must also hate: a man hates damp, a loach hates dryness; water and fire check each other, cold and heat grind each other — such is the principle. What difficulty is there? The dragon loves to hide and hates to be seen; it fears metal and iron and dreads bells and drums. So when its body is touched it trembles, when its ear is touched it shakes, when its mind is touched it submits. Hence the ancients who tamed dragons always used an iron-bound bowl, and so could tame its nature and hide its form. Hence by sound one enters along with it and it is transformed; thus one may keep it in the palm, companion its shadow, and never leave it. Its secret is nothing else: gaining its nature. The same applies to land. I have privately observed the force of this great prefecture: its mountains and waters leap like a flying dragon — how easy to control? So on the upper reach of the eastern river they needled it with the Yanxiang Stūpa: this is the hundred meetings. On the right flank of the western river they needled it with the Renhe Stūpa: this is the waist shu. As for Shuixi, it is the gate of life. The hermitage is named Jilong, Gathering the Dragon — how could that be without meaning? It is like the vessels of the whole body gathered at the gate of life, wrapping the sea of qi and pouring in the essence, the most essential point. A pity its scale is small and insufficient to meet it, like a great body with thin qi, a deep illness with a weak dose. And moreover it leaks away at the tail gate — how can it be easily settled? Hence of old it was twice nearly ruined and twice revived; the force of circumstances made it so. Now the water mouth of the three peaks is like the tail gate; lately a stūpa court was built to press it down, like a gate of defense. Ah, this undertaking — who but one with the Dharma-eye who wields the art of taming dragons could take part in it? The moxa applied by this stūpa is like blocking the tail gate to gather the gate of life, to fill the essence and preserve the primal qi; it is truly bound up with the life and death of this great prefecture — how much more than mere weal and woe. If one could widen its foundation and enlarge its scale, set the bells and drums sounding and the voices reciting the sūtras, pour out sincerity to reach the gods, so that the dragon hears and submits, heaven hears and rejoices, men hear and are transformed, and creatures touched by it flourish; so that rain and sunshine come in season and calamity and evil omens cease; so that the people are blessed through a billion ages, the imperial plan prayed for in eternal firmness, and this land preserved without bound — seen thus, the gathering of blessing is the gathering of the dragon. The hermitage is named Jilong because the dragon gathers here. The founding of the hermitage cannot be traced. In the early Longqing era the monk Zhenliang dwelt there in hardship, and with the funds from reciting sūtras bought several mu of monk-supporting land; before long he passed away and his disciples could not keep it. When I dwelt at Wuyang my disciple Rujian came here to rest and knelt reciting the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, toiling bitterly three years, and the people of the prefecture believed and revered him; he wished to leave but they pressed him to stay, so he greatly renewed it, and after three more years the work was barely complete. In the winter of the guimao year I went to Caoxi to serve the Sixth Patriarch and passed by this hermitage myself, and knew that it was important not only for one prefecture but was the crossroads of the wanderers beyond the ridges. And I would again gather the wanderers as the dragon’s life-vein, so that the numinosity of the mountains and rivers, having found its man to assist it, may spread the rain of Dharma over sands of the Ganges and moisten the numinous root through vast kalpas; and its benefit is not set up for one prefecture or one man alone. Surveying this land, in ten days I gained its outline; by the smallness of this hermitage I would figure the greatness of the mountains and rivers, and directly bring out what lies hidden, to tell those who have not heard.
The Dream Wanderings Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Twenty-Four
Record of Exploring the Wonders of the Qiong Sea

In the tenth year of my exile, in the third month of the spring of the yisi year of Wanli, I took my staff from Leiyang and traveled south to Tianchi to explore the wonders of the Qiong Sea and to keep my appointment with the Master of Rites Lord Wang and the remonstrating counselor Lord Xu. I lodged at the Mingchang Stūpa Court. The court was proposed and built by Lord Xu to make up for the deficiency of the northeast quarter of the prefectural city. It stands alone in mid-heaven, towering to the Milky Way; climbing it and looking round, one seems to ride the cool wind and wander the empty sea, the sound of the tide shaking the heavens and the water’s color clear and void, again like the music of heaven overlooking a bright mirror. Majestic, it is a great wonder. I stayed ten days, and my disciples came daily in greater numbers; we lingered on the tower and discoursed on the Way at leisure. The scholar Chen Yuchen invited me to seek Vimalakīrti’s golden grain and Master Su’s white dragon, and we found the truth of both, and were glad and forgot to return. Some days later the adjutant Liu took me wandering on the West Lake to see the Jade Dragon Spring, and gladly I ordered my staff. It was the tenth day of the first month of summer. The lake lies twenty li or so west of the prefecture. Ridges and hills spread out, and as far as the eye reaches all is dark green. Pointing to the Stone Mountain we went south twenty li, and three li or so out of the city wall: village gardens and vegetable plots linked in rows like scales, stones piled into banks and earth split into beds, bone exposed and flesh hidden, lean without and rich within, with sorghum, millet, beans, and wheat, fine vegetables and small grains — all five grains complete and dazzling to the eye, just like the Western Hills of Jimen. Winding and turning we gradually entered deep forest, walked several li with dense growth covering the wilds so that one could not tell high from low, threaded the clouds and trod the stones, and stepped out at a small brook. The clear stream mirrored a man so that a hair could be counted; heart and spleen were washed clean and the scorching heat at once revived me. Not a few dozen paces and we came to a great stream; crossing a stone bridge we bent over the flow and washed our hair, and our flesh and bones rose in goose bumps. Then dragging my staff I strolled, and heard a dog bark in the clouds without seeing any smoke or fire. A small turn brought us into a village, the dwellings walled all round, every wall built of piled stone, plain in shape and ancient in color, with grey moss and green vines trailing and crossing over them like strings of pearls hung on a heavenly crown. I was glad and forgot weariness, and leaning on my staff entered a gate. After a long while an old man came out: long brows and heavy head, wearing a cow-nose loincloth, in worn clothes and with a dirty face, his elbows showing through his pulled-together lapels; he looked as though he did not see us, and when questioned did not answer, blank as one who has forgotten, and turning his head went back in. From this I knew that the men of Qin are not only in Wuling. I stood a while, then stroking my beard gave a long whistle and went out west of the village. The stones grew larger and the forest deeper; stone banks lined the brook, and then we saw rich soil and level fields, rice like clouds, with flowing water poured in, swirling and surrounding it, like the Wei River and the Qi’ao — only I regretted there were no cloud-touching tall bamboos. Coconuts, palms, and betel nut towered to the sky in every place, such as the world does not have and Qi’ao cannot easily match. Dragging my clogs I followed the stream, threading fields and crossing hollows without telling east from west. After several more li I crossed a small brook and climbed a level ridge, and knew we had turned west. Thorns caught at our clothes and forest grass blocked the road; we parted the clouds and pushed aside the mist, climbed the vines and trod the steps, joyful in spirit and strong on foot. Passing more than ten li, all was stone piled into banks, like balls, like fists, like leather balls, like tables, great and small, leaning and sidelong, some square as if cut, some slanting like walls, built into dikes and rings, dense as a net’s mesh, ranged in natural cliffs, all without missing the mark; some as large as a ten-foot chamber, some rocky as a palace wall, and some that ten thousand men could not lift, heaped and hanging, so that I suspected it was the work of ghosts. Climbing high and gazing far, the fields were joined all across the wilds and everywhere the same — how strange. Lingering and looking about, faintly above the tips of the brushwood they rose in uneven rows like layer upon layer of city wall, and looking round all was vast, silent without human sound, deep and far withdrawn — not the human world. Turning a little north, I saw far off among the clouds a pillar, which my followers pointed out as the Stone Lake; I privately doubted it. Its stones are spread over the ground, level as a palm, colored like old iron, wondrous in shape, the large like a lotus platter, the small like a bee’s cell; strange forms and varied shapes, and walking on we could not see their tracks. Turning a little we entered a stone gate; a narrow path wound on, and only then did I know it was one stone formed by nature, several tens of li around, high on all four sides, with a lake hollowed in the middle, like a bright mirror held up to the sky, and again like a glass cup set in a living pond; who hollowed it, no one knows. It is said that this place was formerly inhabited, and that one day wind and thunder rose greatly, a dragon came out of the stone, great waters boiled up, and the houses were all drowned to make the lake; when heaven is dry the water dries, and the stone has a dragon’s shape. Once in a great drought it appeared in a dream to the prefect and said: I am the dragon of Stone Lake; pray to me and you shall have rain. The prefect went and prayed and it answered at once, and he built a temple to sacrifice to it; to this day it has become the custom. A hundred paces into the stone gate we crossed a small bridge; there was a pool, with old trees above it like a spread canopy, and below it an old hall of three bays whose beams were all of stone. Behind the hall was a pool, inscribed Jade Dragon Spring; above the pool was an old shrine of three bays, which is the image of the Jade Dragon’s spirit maiden. On the left is the Dragon Spring, coming out from a crack in the stone, spurting like pearls, as thick as a cart axle, pouring into a square pool; above the pool are the foundations of a pavilion, below it a long bay, all with their old stories, now lost. East of the pool a small stone ridge divides it; below the ridge is a brook called Huang Creek. Looking down from the brook, jagged and steep, within the hollow stones, like platters and pools, are many wonders, but the forest grass screens them so that one cannot enter. The water gathers into a stream, winding and hidden, meeting in a single opening; and they say it comes out at the stone bridge of the village in front, winding round the foot of ten thousand hills, threading fields and crossing gorges, passing outside Stone Tower Mountain, through the prefecture gate to the south, crossing the Xiangshui Bridge, and then straight east to join the great river and pour into the sea. The adjutant Tang and the two scholars Huang and I washed our feet in the clear stream, let down our hair and opened our robes, and sat at ease above the pool. A cool wind came from every side and our hair and bones were refreshed, as though sitting in the Guanghan palace facing an ice jar and looking into a jade mirror, quite unaware that this was the hot wilderness and the pestilential sea. At dusk we turned back, and following the watercourse I looked: it comes from its source out of the valley, winds west and skirts south, and goes straight east into the river, seemingly having no connection with the prefectural city. We returned at the day’s end, and lying in the high tower I seemed to dream the journey; waking, I recorded it. And so I discussed it, saying: Qiong’s vein comes from the central plain, turning from Nanyue to western Yue, drawing a branch down to Guilin, where the left and right rivers escort it south; at Cangwu and Gui waters it crosses a gorge, winds out to Ling, and at Qin enters the sea as Peng-hu; turning to Zhuya it suddenly wells up, with Five Fingers piercing the sky, facing north toward the central plain, the lock and key of the southern region, encircling three thousand li: truly a great wonder of heaven and earth. Our Sage Ancestor said: The southern sea is vast; within it are several thousand li of wondrous country — was he not a heaven-eye? I have surveyed the world’s geography: south of Mount Heng the ridge divides into the five ranges, and mountains and waters turn their backs on China and race south into the sea. Thus in the great form about the sea, Korea is on the left and Annam on the right like two wings; Japan, Luzon, Siam, and the islands are ranged without; and the Qiong country stands exactly as the shield of the hundred Yue, truly a great metropolis beyond the sea. Five Fingers arch back, rising alone in mid-heaven as Qiong’s ancestral dragon; the mountain faces north and the water flows north, its waist knotted at Ding’an. The water turns left and right, following the dragon and hastening, spanning the east of the prefecture and going straight into the sea. The mountain then runs right, following the western sea north to knot at Stone Mountain, lifting its head and opening its mouth, spitting out the true vein from its midst, coiling and falling east, looking back like the bright pearl beneath a wandering dragon’s jaw, and knotting into the prefectural city. Stone Mountain is the head, its left lip opening into the sea as the rear support, with a small stream following it; on the right it trails a long ridge, several tens of li square, with Stone Lake in the middle, winding south; the cross ridge is the prefecture, and behind the ridge table is the White Water, tightly wrapping the trunk dragon. From Stone Tower it circles the southwest corner of the city, passes the gate and turns left, gathering low as the South Lake; while Stone Lake’s water flows outside and wraps within, crossing the Xiangshui Bridge. Of old it went from Mapo northeast, circling the Spring Ox House, gathering the East Lake and turning northwest, turning from the New Bridge to meet the White Water, embracing the east of the city and turning. Now it turns back and leaps straight in; the river is like a bow, turning its back on the prefectural city and never looking at it, which is what geomancers call the qi dispersed. Lord Xu built the Mingchang Stūpa in the northeast to block the water mouth, and proposed to lead the water of Stone Lake around the south of the city and embrace the eastern suburb, to meet the White Dragon and Golden Grain and pass Mingchang before entering the river, so as to complete the living qi — truly a work of nature. In the end it was not done; was it blocked by men? I sat on the tower and every night climbed the stūpa, and seeing the qi of the mountains and rivers so bleak, I pointed and said to the disciples who followed me: Qiong will surely have a calamity, for the mountains and rivers are desolate and the city seems empty of men — this is to have no qi. At the time they thought it nonsense. On the sixteenth day of the first month of summer I crossed the sea and returned north. Before a month had passed the earth shook greatly: the east gate split and the city sank, the houses all collapsed, officials and people camped in the open, and the stūpa too leaned by half; the tower I dwelt in also rocked and tossed, and I was unquiet for half a year. To this day those who remember my words take them as proof. So I record it together.
Record of the Golden Grain Spring in Qiongzhou (with Inscription)

The prefecture of Qiong is about ten li from the sea. In the northeast corner of the city, at the foot of a ridge and the instep of the water, there is a spring that wells up grain, grain upon grain glistening like pearls floating on the sea’s eye. Men take it and test it: husked, it gives white kernel, just like the northern buckwheat; and when winter comes and the qi gathers and the spring grows warm, the grain sprouts like rice shoots pricking the water — so it is truly not a phantom product. The people of the time found it strange and wondered, not knowing whence it came, and generally called it the Grain Spring. In the third month of the spring of the yisi year of Wanli I crossed the sea from Leiyang to visit the Master of Rites Lord Wang and the remonstrating counselor Lord Xu, and to explore the wonders of the Qiong Sea. The scholar Chen Yuchen, a man of broad culture, came to see me at the Mingchang Stūpa Court and invited the Master of Rites to come with him to the abbot’s quarters of Tianning; over tea we spoke of this, and so we took our staffs and went to see it. I had a servant search in the sand and mud, and he did indeed get several grains of millet, and rubbing off the husk brought out rice like a new harvest. I found it most strange, and named it the Golden Grain Spring, taking the sense of Vimalakīrti, the Golden Grain Tathāgata — Li Bai called himself his later body — which seemed to fit the Master of Rites as a scholar. We drew water and boiled tea; the taste was very cold and clear, and drinking it made hair and bones cool, as though in Vimalakīrti’s chamber eating the fragrant rice. The scholar Chen harbored doubt and left his mat to ask: Grain is produced in the northern land and the spring wells up in the southern heaven, ten thousand li apart and separated by the sea crossing — how has it come here? This a wise man must doubt and common feeling cannot fathom. I beg to ask the reason. I said: Ha, this is hard to speak of with the common. Let me try to discuss it. The great earth floats on water like a single leaf; the water flows secretly beneath the lands of the four continents as a man’s blood vessels pour through his whole body. It is born from the heart and nourishes the five viscera, reaches outward to the four limbs, penetrates the skin, goes down to the bubbling spring and up to the crown, and there is no hair, nail, or tooth that is not filled; if not filled, there is no feeling. Seen thus, heaven and earth are one finger, the ten thousand things one body. Water and fire shoot at each other, mountain and marsh communicate their qi, wind and cloud breathe, the tide swallows and spits, heaven and earth open and shut, day and night come and go, with not a moment’s pause — just like a man’s daily eating, breathing, rising and resting. What is strange in it? Long ago a spirit-monk came from the Western Regions and drank the water of Caoxi, fragrant and sweet, and cried in wonder: This is the water of my Baolin in the western heaven. In the Great Compassion Tower at Zhongshan, the tower a hundred feet high and the image eight zhang, a strange monk of the Tang converted gold, coin, copper, and wood everywhere and stored them in a well; and when he returned and took them out, they all came forth from the well, enough for his use — and to this day one piece of wood remains. Seen thus, the waters of the great earth have never been unconnected, nor things unreached; this is a plain fact. Long ago Su the Elder, dwelling at Dan’er, once judged the springs of the three mountains and said they were connected with Hui Mountain, and so named it the Hui Passage Spring. Thus the great void is vast and the ten thousand forms merge and pass through; it is only that men have obstructions in their minds. I observe that in the Qiong Sea the land rises in the northwest and its qi knots in the southeast, like the nail of a man’s finger. The nail is the surplus of the sinews; blood nourishes the sinews, and when the sinews are firm the nail is thick. Whoever has thick nails must be long-lived; hence where the soil is thick there must be many talents. Those who speak say that the soil of the central plain is thick, and so generals and ministers mostly come from there. I say otherwise. Qiong lies in the south, in the li. The li is the body of the qian: drawing in one yin, hard without and soft within, empty and brightly shining — the image of culture and brightness. Its land floats in the sea, fire and metal produce water, and so the day is hot and the night cold. Because the true qi of heaven and earth reaches its extreme here and is concentrated here, the gold, silver, and bright pearls of its mountains and rivers, its patterned birds and famous fragrance, its rare and strange beasts, its hidden treasures all arise here and the hundred things are complete; and among men, immortals and numinous ones, men of literary fame, loyal ministers and righteous scholars, come forth from time to time. This is one corner of heaven and earth, like one mote in the great void; transformation shifts in secret and the dull do not perceive it. It has briefly sent up one grain to show it, like judging spring and autumn from a single leaf. What is strange in it? The Master of Rites heard this and leaped with joy, and sighed again, saying: How wonderful. Those present, the scholar Shen Chengde and others, bowed again and again and asked me to inscribe it, to enlighten those who have not heard. So I made this inscription, saying:

The great earth is one mote, the vast sea one grain; filling the ten directions, what is lacking anywhere? Like a hair on the body, like blood through the whole frame: wherever touched it appears — where is it not true? Kan and Li, water and fire; heaven and earth are in me. Their meeting and engendering — what could prevent it? The earth’s qi comes from the north and gathers in the south; things follow it and well up in between. Men doubt this grain and do not know whence it comes; not knowing its origin, how shall they make clear the doctrine? Transformation shifts in secret, beyond hearing and seeing; let us borrow one grain to observe its changes. If one knows one grain, a mustard seed contains the void; water and fire pervade all — how could they not hold each other? The blood vessels run through the body from crown to toe, flowing up and down, ending and beginning again. The great Way circles and nothing goes that does not return; the Way-vein secretly passes through, like this one grain. The deep spring flows on and from time to time sends it forth; that the Way-vein comes south may be divined from this.
Record of a Visit to Jingtai Temple

The mountains and rivers of Guangdong rise from Mount Heng, break at the Yu Ridge and come down, knotting at the waist in Caoxi, winding south until they reach Wuyang. The master mountain of Wuyang is Yuexiu, and the ancestral dragon of Yuexiu is White Cloud. White Cloud has many wonders, and Jingtai is the finest, for it sits in White Cloud’s belly and strokes the city of the immortal dragon; its two wings embrace, like an old oyster holding a pearl. Lone peaks and sheer ravines, deep groves dense, rare flowers and strange herbs, mist and cloud coming and going; calamus grows in the cracks of the rocks, and palm fronds spread above the forest. The great sea is like a mirror standing at one’s brow, and the bright moon like a pearl whose light flows upon one’s lips. Truly a wonder of heaven and earth and a grand beauty of the southern sea. At first the temple took its name from the mountain; in the Jingtai era of our Ming it petitioned for and was granted its name as before, and the governor Lord Ma Ang with his subordinates renewed it. I dwelt at Wuyang three years; in the wuxu year I took my Chan companions to visit, and it was of the utmost excellence. In mid-spring of the dingwei year I received the imperial command to return to the mountains, and the temple monk Zhengyi brought me this picture with a request; so I have written a brief record.
Record of the Baoyue Terrace in Duanzhou

According to the gazetteer, a hundred and fifty paces north of the prefecture is the Baoyue Terrace, rising abruptly from level ground, two zhang high and a li or so around, which viewed from afar is like a terrace. It is natural, not man-made; but when it was first named is unknown. High banks and deep valleys change without constancy, and it is now a level lake and dike: perhaps a man of power carried it off, and the mountains and rivers are as they were, with no true master any more. In the jiachen year of Wanli the provincial vice-commissioner Lord Chen of Lingxi, in his leisure from governing the prefecture, made a circuit of its fair prospects, and climbing high and gazing far he sighed and said: Now I know that the Baoyue Terrace stands at the heart of the level lake. In the geomancers’ art a dwelling must have something to lean on; the Star Rocks are indeed the prefecture’s screen, but pressed in front and loose behind. Heaven made this land as the throat of the ridges and the crossroads of the hundred Yue; measured by wind and qi, how could it be so open and leaking? So I know beyond doubt that this terrace is, in the geomancers’ phrase, the ghost’s trust of the prefectural city. Can it be left to perish forever? So he proposed to raise a dike and build a terrace at the lake’s heart to make it solid. Workmen were gathered and the work done, finished in no time. Lord Feng Yuancheng of Huating, transferring from the Zhejiang commission to this land, climbed the terrace and looked all round, and said: Beautiful it is, but not yet complete. A dike made into a terrace does not answer to the name; the moon is round and the square is the rule, and the likeness loses the truth — this is man not yet matching heaven. Moreover a mountain is famous if it has an immortal, and water is numinous if it has a dragon: this speaks of gaining its master. Therefore whoever builds a work of lasting and unshakable merit must have it made by man and guarded by spirits, relying on a constant master and not losing its sacrifice; then it can be as long-enduring as heaven and earth. So the Lord donated his salary and, at the central bay of the terrace hall, made an image of the White-Robed Great Being, wearing strings of pearls and overlooking the empty water, sitting in the burning house and sprinkling coolness, upright as pure crystal holding the jewel moon. I was honored by the Lord’s invitation, and so discussed with him how to supply what was lacking before: afterward to build a five-bay pavilion with two bell and drum towers in front, taking the round form to figure the moon and the elevation like a terrace, relying on the Great Being’s numinosity to master it. Only then could one say heaven and man joined in virtue, restoring the whole work of transformation. The Lord gladly donated his salary, and the work was begun, starting in the tenth month of the winter of the dingwei year of Wanli and completed in the seventh month of the autumn of the wushen year. Its scale is grand and spacious, rising above mid-heaven: painted beams joining the clouds, red pillars mirroring the sun. I climbed it then and looked round on the scene, and in lofty reverie said: How fair is the firmness of the mountains and rivers, how strange the wonder of nature’s making. And I thought that when the terrace was first named it must have been by a geomancer with the Dharma-eye. I have at leisure surveyed the coming dragon of eastern Yue: it takes distant origin in Mount Heng, draws its trunk down, crosses Huai and pours in four directions; Dinghu is the ancestral dragon of Duanzhou, towering into the clouds, winding west, with ranged screens spread wide and the bright hall broad and level, its walls answering the Purple Tenuity, blending and knotting into the Seven Stars. Wondrous peaks and cave chambers in a thousand forms and ten thousand shapes; patterned cliffs and brocade stones steaming with cloud and blazing with haze; a fistful of rock or a single stone is enough to be a treasure of the world. This is the essence of transformation and the hidden depth of mountains and rivers. The Star Rocks are ranged about, fine as spider silk and wandering ants, adorning the level plain; eastward it turns at the Antelope Gorge as Duan’s gate of defense, and on the left goes against the stream upstream; from Huanggang it turns west and knots into the prefectural city. Examining the forms and their principle, it is the returning dragon looking back at its ancestor, turning to gaze at the Seven Stars; and what the gazetteer calls this terrace, rising abruptly on level ground, is it not the pearl beneath the black dragon’s jaw? The meaning takes the pearl of the bright moon as the world’s supreme treasure; hence it is named Baoyue, Precious Moon — how apt. Moreover when nature’s cunning can be taken and figured, that is already wonderful; but when the spirit pearl was lost, Wuxiang sought it and found it in the deep abyss, restoring it to the work of transformation — that is another wonder. To supply what was lacking and draw it out, to give it spirit and clarity and make it a constant guard: this undertaking gathered the excellence of the gentlemen and officials of a whole age, and in a glance its beauty flows through ten thousand ages. This is what is called awaiting its man to flourish, the substance of benevolence and wisdom — how could it be by chance? Water is numinous through its dragon, and the dragon is spirit-like through its pearl; and he who rides the dragon, locks horns with it, seizes its jaw, and strips its scales to snatch the pearl — that is the man. So this land has long been numinous. The terrace is flanked by two temples, Hui Ri on the left and Jing Ming on the right, like day and night taking each other’s place, illumining the deluded quarters and breaking the heavy dark; bells and drums mingle and the tide’s sound plays in turn, above praying for the emperor’s long life and below blessing the people. Loyalty, filial piety, chastity, and righteousness rise with the times — truly by the Great Being’s numinosity. As for settling this land to press down Hua and Yi and spreading the wind of compassion to aid the imperial rule, that is truly a benefit of ten thousand ages without end — how could it be worth no more than the beauty of a view? This is the record.
Record of a Dream Journey to Duan Creek

In mid-summer of the jiyou year of Wanli, on the twelfth day of the fifth month, I was at Duanzhou gathering timber for the restoration of Baolin, coming and going for a year; when the work was done I returned to the mountain. It was the height of the damp heat, and heavy rains fell; the river rose in flood, and on either bank and islet one could not tell ox from horse. So we let the boat go with the current, down the Antelope Gorge and past the mouth of Duan Creek. Suddenly the clouds closed on the four mountains and wind and rain came whistling; the waves surged so that the boat could not advance, and we moored to avoid it. My spirit shook and my eyes swam, and leaning on the armrest I dozed, and dreamed a journey. I looked up at peaks wondrous and fair, piercing the upper heavens; strange rocks jagged, overlooking a bottomless void. Far off I heard the creek rushing and dashing, striking the crevices and battering the cliffs, like striking a great bell or beating an alligator drum, the sound coming from heaven, rumbling and hollow, no one knew from where. I thought it must be the lair of a flood-dragon or the cave dwelling of a spirit man, the sound of footsteps in an empty valley. I was delighted at the sound and called the fisherman to pole the boat into the creek to let my eyes wander. After a while wind and rain stopped for a time, the mist gathered and the mountain cleared. I tucked up my robe, went barefoot, and dragging my staff threaded the clouds. Turning a little along the creek, more than a hundred paces brought me to the mountain’s foot, where there was a spirit altar; I paid reverence among the wild brambles and rested a while on a stone. A few dozen paces on I heard near at hand a strange sound as though issuing from the air. I stood long, looking round in a daze, peering at the hanging cliffs and gazing into the dark ravine, and at last traced whence the sound came. The fisherman said: This is the Small Rock of Duan Creek, the very place that produces the famous inkstones. The cave is full of water, with one opening like a mouth; at first hearing, its sound is like a lion’s roar, then many sounds jostle like a crowd crying and running, great and small, like thunder and lightning, like collapse and flight, like pipes and reeds, like metal and stone clanging, like the night cry of the imperial bells — it is the sound of the spring water flowing in the cave. I stood on tiptoe and inclined my ear, and stroking my beard said gladly: Ah, is this not what Zhuangzi called the pipes of earth? How strange are its rare tones and wondrous sounds. Lingering long, I climbed the layered summit on the left and saw on the mountain’s flank something like crenellations: the site of the stone-quarrying office. East over a small ridge a few hundred paces, a ravine entwined it and two ridges spread like wings; on both sides of the ravine the broken stones were heaped like scattered stars and torn brocade spread out — the yard where the stone was cut. Small ones and great, like palms, like fingers, like ears, like teeth, like bees, like butterflies, like wings, like tails, and one could not tell how many tens of millions of pieces. Looking closely at their shapes, they were like cut black jade and severed jasper branches, like clipped cloud and haze scattering figured silk: the spittle cast off from a ten-foot stone, the dross of what had become a useful piece. They could be enjoyed but not grasped, loved but not picked up. My eyes were glad and my spirit wide as I trod; I climbed east, parting thorns and treading the jagged heights, down the ridge and into the creek. The clear stream was like a mirror, every hair countable, one sheet of blue emptiness, with the crowd of peaks reflected. Groping the vines and looking down, a sheer wall faced the stream, deep and still and silent, as though a spirit dragon coiled beneath it. The fisherman pointed and said to me: This is the Great Rock of Duan Creek. I saw only grey vines and green bamboo shading it above, deep and hidden and dim, so that its door could not be made out. The fisherman said: The gate lies at the bottom of the water, sealed by a jumble of stones; even when the government quarries, they wait for the water to dry in the three winter months and then open it. Within it is unfathomable. They hollow the empty and fill the solid, and the gathered water becomes a pool several tens of zhang wide, too deep to cross; above it opens into many crevices, below it joins the tail gate; the tide rises and falls, waxing and waning with the times. Though ten thousand men labored, it would not easily be drained. Even if one worked at it, pumping out the water with carts, laboring from midnight to noon, one would only just see the edge of the cliff, and the stoneworkers would weave baskets of bamboo and take it — not easily got. From this one knows that the Duan inkstone holds water without drinking it because it is born of water. Above the rock’s face the two mountains embrace, and in the middle it is like the hollow of a palm, looking like an ancient grave. It was too high to climb, so I sent a boy to look; there was a stone tablet sealed with moss, its age indistinguishable, on which one could just make out the grave of Chen Mengfu. It is said that an imperial quarrying commissioner of a former dynasty died at his task and was granted burial here, as though to make his spirit keep guard. I sighed and said: The mountains and rivers are as of old; how long is a man’s life — this is the proof. I called the fishing boat, crossed the clear creek, and explored below the rock: the jumbled stones heaped at the bottom of the water are the cave’s door. The wave-light rippled, like flowing haze scattering color on the water; what can be seen but not drawn up is the stone’s lingering blaze and leftover radiance. I loosened my robe and sat at ease, opened my collar and let down my hair, and washed my feet in the clear stream.
