Poling the boat a little forward, the fallen waves and rushing rapids struck the stones and spurted pearls, splashing my face and wetting my hair, so that my hair stood and my skin bristled. The water was shallow and the boat large, and it stuck fast so that we could not go up; so I left the boat and entered the creek, wading and lifting my clothes through the murmuring water, and counted the crowd of stones and sported among them. The jumbled stones were like ants, jagged and toothed: great and small, like sheep, like oxen, like pigs, like dogs, like winnowing baskets, like pecks, like fists, like hands. The great ones had their flesh melted away and their bones exposed, naturally round; the small ones were the leavings of hammer and chisel, worn and polished till they shone, and rolling in the waves with the stubborn stones — they are hard to name. I stroked and played with them all and washed them clean, pulling out hairs and scraping off grime, till they were sleek and lovely and dazzling to see. I sighed in a daze and said: Truly the maker grudges a fair vessel. Thus one knows that the essence of mountains and rivers and the flower of culture are forbidden by Heaven, and the common man cannot seize them. The fisherman with his nets and the woodcutter with his axe pass by dull and unheeding because they have no use for them; and if there are men of ink and brush, historians of the pen, who seek them and cannot find them, long for them and rarely see them, it is because they lodge far away and are not easily known to the world. There are also those who get a mere likeness, whose use does not match the office and whose name falls short of the reality, and so they slander it: purple usurping red. Therefore I urgently ordered the boy to scrape the sand and dig the mud, to choose and select. The great ones were too hard to lift; the small ones filled a handful, perhaps a dozen pieces, and I carried them home in my bosom, like gathering purple mushrooms and picking cloud-petals — truly a joy. Yet they were all the leavings of chipping and slant cutting, unfit for carving; and I treasure them though I know they are useless, because their virtue accords with the noble man, complete in miniature, enough to lodge my heart in and to glimpse one stripe of the work of transformation. Presently wind and rain came rushing, thunder drove and lightning rolled; I knew the mountain spirits would not keep me, so I followed the stream out of the creek and returned to the boat. Suddenly a fierce thunderclap split the mountain, and I started awake, losing at once all that had been before. Pushing back the awning I sighed deeply and looked round at the ten thousand mountains, wrapped in mist and curtained with cloud, the crowd of peaks piercing the sky, grim as halberds. I paced about irresolute; the fish’s tracks and bird’s traces — I fear the wonder-lover in me — wanting to speak of them, my words were lost, and I could not recall them. So I entrusted them to the brush.
Record of the Repair of the Sixth Patriarch’s Hall at Guangxiao Temple in Guangzhou

Long ago, before the Buddha appeared in the world, Prince Jeta of the king of Śrāvastī had a garden of rich beauty, ample for wandering and viewing. When the Buddha appeared, he divined and opened a lecture hall there, and it was chosen as a monastery, and to this day it is called the Jetavana. Thus a man makes a place famous. Zhao Tuo, as commandant of Nanhai, chose the Kesala Grove for his garden. In the Longan era of the Eastern Jin the monk Venerable Dharmayaśas of Kashmir came from the Western Regions and loved the excellence of the place, and so begged it to build a monastery, named the King’s Garden Temple. In the early Yonghe era of the Jin the Tripiṭaka master Guṇabhadra brought the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra from the western land and built a precept platform at that temple to await a sage. In the early Tianjian era of the Liang the Tripiṭaka master Zhiyao of the western heaven brought a branch of the bodhi tree and planted it beside the platform, and recorded it, saying: A hundred and sixty years from now a bodhisattva in a fleshy body will open the Dharma here and save beings without measure. In the Zhenguan era of the Tang the King’s Garden was renamed Faxing Temple; and in the early Longshuo era of Emperor Gaozong, our Great Master the Sixth Patriarch, having received the robe and bowl of Huangmei, hid himself for fifteen years. In the early Yifeng era, through the debate on wind and banner, his talent showed itself; and he was indeed shaved beneath the tree, ascended the platform, and received the precepts, and was acclaimed as teacher of gods and men, fulfilling the hidden prophecy. From then on the Dharma-banner stood at Caoxi and his teaching covered the world; and to this day this place is called the root ground. Yet the Way of the Buddha and the patriarchs is originally non-dual, and so Jetavana and the King’s Garden are one. Is it not that a man is made excellent by the Way and a place is made excellent by the man? I have read Xuanzang’s Record of the Western Regions, which says that the Jetavana monastery is now a field of thorns; and now I see the Kesala Grove and the enlightenment tree and still hear the sound of bells and chanting. Is southern Yue more numinous than the western heaven, or the ancestral Way greater than the Buddhadharma? The sages transmitted to one another and appeared in the world according to the times; at the moment of transmission not an instant could intervene. Only their vow-power differed in depth, and so their conditions of transformation were long or short. It is like the four seasons: when the work is done, the doer withdraws. Thus the voices of transformation await one another — awaiting, and again awaiting, and yet again awaiting; and when there is no awaiting, the traces of responding to conditions are well-nigh stilled. Now we are a thousand years from our Great Master the Sixth Patriarch. Of the thousand seven hundred recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp, the places where they taught rose and fell with the times, and many have sunk away in every quarter. Of the monasteries of Guangdong not one in a hundred survives; yet Caoxi still flows and does not dry, and the enlightenment tree still flourishes and does not wither. Is it not because this Way has something to rely on? This again is a place preserved by the Way and men dwelling by the Dharma. In youth I practiced dry Chan, and for the Dharma I incurred blame. In the early spring of the bingshen year I paid reverence to the Great Master the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi, and gazed on the enlightenment tree at Guangxiao, and sought out the old matters. His traces were remote, and men did not know a monk. Within a year I went begging for food; in three years fasting and precepts were practiced and the releasing of life undertaken; in five years the new precept platform at Caoxi was restored; in ten years the teaching spread widely and those who believed in the Way were many. This was the working of the great wheel of fate. The men of old took the place beneath the bodhi tree as the ground where the Master had his hair shaved, and so built a hall for Dharma services; its coming is far off. Wind and rain wear it away, and it rises and falls with the times. Now the monk Tongwei, with his disciples Xingpei and others, has collected from the public and renewed it. I have cleared its brows and eyes and widened its gates and corridors, so that the Way’s countenance, dim, shines again and the lamp of wisdom, bright, is not darkened. This again is a matter that depends on human effort, and men are made weighty through the matter. Now the Buddha gathered beings by the six perfections, and the perfection of giving is the first; and what is not adornment is named adornment. If the marks of the matter and the Dharma-nature merge and pass through, then conventional truth and suchness interpenetrate, and then burning incense and scattering flowers are all wondrous practice. As for Tongwei, does his carving of rafters and beams not furnish the goods of the Pure Land? Long ago the platform was set and the tree planted, and there was an awaiting of the Sixth Patriarch; now the traces remain and the work is repaired, the man is gone and the Way is here — is there not an awaiting of later men? And the excellence of the King’s Garden, compared with Jetavana, is a going there and a coming here; again there is a difference. This is the record.
Record of the Causes and Conditions of Kaifu Temple in Hengzhou Prefecture

Kaifu Temple stands a li or so from the south bank of the Xiang River by the prefectural city. In the Dali era of the Tang, Chan Master Wuzhu opened the mountain here. The Master’s Dharma lineage is recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp. At first he and Chan Master Fazhao formed a Buddha-recitation society east of the lake, and afterward both traveled to Mount Wu and saw Mañjuśrī face to face, as is fully told in the Qingliang Record. The Master and his younger brother Wujue built bodhimaṇḍas together: the Master founded Kaifu, and Jue founded the Great Compassion Temple at Jinlan in the western district; it was all in one period. Kaifu’s original plan was broad and spacious. In the Chunxi era of the Song the chancellor Lord Zhao Ruyu, posthumously named Zhongding, was banished to Yongzhou and passed through Heng, where he fell ill and was harassed by the prefect Qian Mou, and died suddenly; he was buried here, and a shrine was raised and sacrificed to at the seasons. Later the prefect Lord Xiang Zimin had a beneficent government and kept tens of thousands alive in a year of famine, and the people were moved by him and also raised a shrine here. In time the temple fell into ruin. In the first year of the Yuan there was Chan Master Fuhai, who revived it and also renewed the Great Compassion Temple. In the Xuande era of our Ming the temple fell into ruin again, and the people built a small hermitage on the waste site, only one plot, with a few surviving monks, kept to this day, happily not lost among the people. In the renshen year of Longqing the good men of the prefecture, Qi Xia and others, repaired the hermitage again and had the monk Rulu keep it. In the gengxu year of Wanli the provincial graduate Mr. Du Yougui, whose dwelling was next to the temple, dreamed one night of an old man who mounted a horse and said: I am the earth god of Kaifu. That year Mr. Du passed the provincial examination, and told the dream to his kinsman the Master of Rites Lord Zeng Jinjian. The Lord said: According to the prefectural gazetteer, Kaifu was rebuilt by Chan Master Fuhai; and your style is now Fuhai — are you not his former or later body? You should renew this place, to record that you do not forget your original cause. Mr. Du was glad, and with the good men of the village Liu Zilian, Qi Xia, and the scholar Liu Mingluan and others strove to renew it. The prefectural adjutant Lord Yin, who deeply honored the Three Jewels, strongly took it in hand. Because the ground had long been waste and mostly lost among the people, the site was cramped and the two shrines had sunk away, so that the old state could not be restored. After five or six years of management they built three bays of Buddha hall. Kaifu at the east of the lake is a foot away; Lord Zeng rebuilt the east lake temple and invited me to preside. In the winter of the guichou year I came from Guangdong, and the good men who were managing Kaifu came to ask me to go and look at it. Pitying their hearts and honoring their will, I wrote this record for them, saying: From ancient times the places where Buddhas and patriarchs taught the Dharma, the bodhimaṇḍas they built, were bound in the diamond realm, and all had dragon spirits and Dharma-protectors to guard them, so that even through the end of the kalpa they are not extinguished. Long ago the World-Honored One, walking in order with Indra, pointed to a place and said: This is where the seven Buddhas of the past taught the Dharma; a monastery should be built here. Then the elder Xianyu at once planted a stalk in the ground and said: The monastery is built. This is the proof. Since the Buddhadharma came to China, the monasteries of the world have stood in every quarter like jeweled palaces, scattered like stars and chessmen; and though they fall into the wild thickets their names do not decay, and whoever revives them brings out what was hidden as though looking on an old possession. This is because cause and effect cannot be effaced. Thus Xu Xun built a stūpa and died before it was finished; later Pei Du became chancellor and visited the temple, and the abbot at one look said: Xu Xuandu, why have you come so late? The stūpa of former days is now as of old. Pei Du heard these words and repaired it, and the stone carving within the stūpa indeed bore the prophecy of a chancellor in red robes. Seen thus, Kaifu lay waste more than a thousand years, and Lord Yin with Lords Zeng and Du initiated its revival; all had great causes with the Buddha-ground, and it was no accident. Formerly Wuzhu and Fazhao began their careers east of the lake and both traveled to Mount Wu and saw Mañjuśrī face to face. Now I began my career at Mount Wu and have come to old age east of the lake, and it happens that I meet the day of Kaifu’s revival. These men coming and going, appearing and vanishing in a snap of the fingers, have never departed from Mañjuśrī’s Bamboo Grove Monastery in the Diamond Cave — three-three before, three-three after. The meeting of causes and conditions, how can it be conceived? Good men, sacrifice to Lord Yin in this temple, and it will be a sign for a later Xuandu and a proof of Mr. Du’s dream of Fuhai. The ring in the mulberry grove is the more clearly without error. So I have set out the whole course in outline to tell those who come. The proverb says: A thousand years of field, eight hundred masters. Those who now praise and rejoice — are they not the Dharma-protectors of later days? The merit of the field of blessing surely has that which does not perish. Can one not believe it?
Record of a Visit to Zhi Mountain

I was hiding at Linghu in Heng when someone spoke of the wondrous beauty of Zhi Mountain in Yongzhou, and my heart longed for it. In the autumn of the yimao year, in the ninth month, Lord Feng, assistant administrator, moved his command from Wuling to Hunan and took up his post at Yongzhou, and invited me on a journey to the Nine Doubts. I arrived at the month’s end, and saw the clear excellence of Yong’s mountains and rivers, like an immortal capital or a cave dwelling, not to be judged by the common world. I lodged on the western bank of the Xiao River in a small tower above the rock, sitting to view the excellence of river and mountain as though they were on my table. On the ninth day of the tenth month of winter the provincial graduate Tang Huanhe and the scholar Lü Xugu invited Zhou Bokong of Tanzhou, Zhang Hancha of Siming, and my Lingnan disciple the monk Chaoyi to visit Zhi Mountain together. Cold rain had fallen for days; then it cleared a little, so dragging our staffs we went from the bank of the West River, and following the edge a li or so came to the mountain’s foot and wound upward. Another li and we climbed a small ridge and saw the crowding peaks, steep and lofty, unclimbable; so we went down the ridge into the valley two hundred paces, turned a little west, and there a wondrous peak rose alone, its hanging cliffs fair and sheer, with a Brahma hall of flying eaves set into the rock: Zhi Mountain Temple, founded and opened in the yisi year of Wanli by the monk Mingjue. Before the temple there is no spare ground, for the dragon’s head blocks it, and one cannot view it at large. Turning west again there is the Guanyin Pavilion, leaning below the high cliff, and there all is open and bright, with the crowd of mountains arrayed as though at one’s lashes; below are level fields and rich soil and a winding stream with nine turns like a sheep’s gut, like a heavenly robe flying its sash, fluttering into one’s bosom, and from the mountain’s foot entering the river. Turning west a few paces again there is a hall of one bay where the three great beings were formerly molded, destroyed by an icchantika; the place is of the deepest beauty, with a cave chamber behind it where several men may sit. Turning west once more, we threaded the jagged stones and climbed up through a crevice; winding up several dozen steps brought us to the mountain’s waist, a level space several zhang across where the former prefect Lord Wang built an empty pavilion, and travelers who reach it may sit and take their pleasure. Wondrous peaks and strange rocks stand ranged about in a thousand forms and ten thousand shapes that cannot be named, like heaped Taihu stones, piled and built in layers, like jade flowers and jewel hearts with dense leaves in bloom. To the left of the pavilion we climbed along the cliff, and the heart of the cave dazzled the eye, like parting a green lotus and drawing out a jeweled heart beyond counting. Above again are two stones like hands, named the Joined Palms Rock, with a cave door below, naturally pierced through; passing the door and going up we came to the Jade Emperor Hall. At one view from here the mountains and rivers on all four sides lie at the bottom of the eye, the city walls spread out like a painting, and the whole excellence of Yong is seen without remainder. I privately think that Master Liu of Yongzhou, who dwelt here more than ten years and explored every hidden place, never set foot here — how did he slight it? Some point to this as the Western Mountain of which Liu wrote; going west from the Ran Creek he also says it stands out alone, which seems to be what is now called the True Pearl Ridge. Others point to it as Qunyu Mountain, and the gazetteer speaks of the Immortal Cave, but below this mountain there is no immortal cave; both are wrong. I say this mountain was unfortunate not to meet Liu, and Liu did not reach this mountain and so did not exhaust it; perhaps the maker secretly guarded it and it awaited this day. I and the others sighed in chorus, saying: The mountains and rivers keep their fair traces; we again climb and look. We strolled slowly and went back seeking Liu’s crag.
Record of the Gaoyun Mountain Buddhist Retreat in Yizhang

Among the famous mountains of the realm, those that gather the essence of heaven and earth, heroic, numinous, and wondrously fair, the Five Peaks are the honored ones; their branches divide in four directions, and Caoxi has its root in Nanyue. Nanyue and Caoxi look at each other across more than a thousand li, their peaks stretching on in a range, ranged like stars. From the time the Sixth Patriarch opened the teaching and Master Rang divided the stream, the Way-vein has run through the world; and above and below Shaoyang there have been more than ten great beings in flesh bodies, and those who to this day seem alive — are they not the hidden depth of the mountains and rivers? Hence the Way-vein has something to rely on especially. Yizhang lies between Cao and Heng; thirty li west of the seat of government is a mountain named Gaoyun, a grandson of Zhurong. It has been numinous long. In the jiaxu year of Jiajing the local man of the Ouyang family founded a hermitage and invited Master Jinhai of Shajin to dwell there, and enlarged the Brahma halls to settle the great assembly; the whole county took refuge in it as a field of blessing, and set aside eight pecks of incense-and-lamp grain. Before long it met with fire; Master Hai departed and hid at Mount Zhiti in Fujian. His disciples Wudan and the others with single strength rebuilt it, and in the renwu year the work was completed; a stūpa was built on the dragon’s head and the Master’s sacred bones were brought back and enshrined. He is the founding patriarch. His disciples advanced daily, and none who came and went between Cao and Heng in the ten directions failed to stop there. The county man Yuan Wenxian donated thirty mu of land to supply the gruel and rice for the wanderers; and from this all quarters praised it. Once the monks had gathered, even the common folk in the deep mountains and poor valleys all knew there were Buddhas and monks; only they had not yet heard that there was a Dharma. There was a Dharma-grandson Xingcheng who resolved to seek the great canon at Jinling, and with bitter heart for twelve years his vow was at last fulfilled. In the sixth month of the summer of the jiyou year of Wanli he brought the great canon home, and the four assemblies joyfully beheld it as though the white horse had come from the west. The hermitage sits on the mountain top, its groves dense, with mist and cloud steaming damp; fearing the canon could not long endure, the Dharma-grandson Zhengui and others proposed to build a pavilion at the mountain’s foot, called Nanzhuang. At that time the magistrate Lord Zheng and the garrison officer Lord Tong were the benefactors who initiated it, and issued letters of faith to tell the four quarters; those who heard rejoiced, and those who came to take refuge did so like a market. The work began in such a year and month and was completed in such a year and month. They were about to open a Dharma assembly and present the water-and-land rite to proclaim benefit and salvation — truly a great bodhimaṇḍa. When the matter was accomplished, the Master’s disciple Wushao, who had followed me to Caoxi, begged words from me, and I recorded it, saying: The ancients said: The whole ten directions is the land of eternal quiescent light; the whole great earth is the true sūtra of universal vision. Then the Buddha-land is pure without being cultivated, and the sūtra scrolls are clear without being unrolled. Yet it is truly because the mind is pure that the land appears, and the eye is clear that the Dharma is manifest. This is what is called: a man can make the Way great, but the Way does not make a man great. The bodhimaṇḍa of Gaoyun and the great canon come from the east — had not Master Hai begun it, his descendants continued the work, and the benefactors completed it, how could brambles have been turned into jewel trees and gravel into a Brahma palace? Now that the Dharma-banner stands and the Way’s course is broadly opened, the green hills and white clouds are the ever-abiding dharma-body; the gibbons’ song and the birds’ clamor ever proclaim the wondrous verse; and the flowing water and moving wind put forth a broad long tongue, singing without end with the people of this place. All who see, hear, and rejoice are like Sudhana entering Maitreya’s adorned tower. This merit — how can the tip of a single hair contain its measure? This is the record.
Record of Lord Mu the Sixth of Lijiang’s Reverence for the Buddha

I was about to retire in old age to Nanyue, and happened to hide at Linghu in Heng. Mr. Feng Yuancheng, transferred to govern Hunan, visited Yongzhou, and speaking of his former travels and the fair sights of southern Yunnan he brought out the Wuling draft. I read the life of Lord Mu the Sixth, and learned that west of the Golden Horse and Green Rooster mountains there is a rare man, Lord Mu the Sixth. The Lord governed Lijiang, holding its territory in full; six transmissions brought it to the Lord, and so he is called the Sixth Lord. His ancestors at the founding of the dynasty rose by loyalty and obedience, most renowned in military merit; down to Lord Xueshan the family became famous for letters, with elegant songs and poems, graceful and soaring with a spirit beyond the clouds, and the court historian Yang Shen greatly praised him. Tradition carried it to Yulong and Songhe, whose writings and letters were of a transcendent order, and who in the Pure Lotus Society cultivated purity and first set foot on the road of enlightenment. By Lord Mu the Sixth all former worthies were far surpassed, and he stood out beyond the dust. The Lord’s nature is plain and thin; for the flavors of the world he has no liking at all. Loyal, filial, compassionate, and loving, he takes only the benefiting of men and things as his heart. He has turned his mind to the Three Jewels and set his will on dhyāna, delighting to receive Dharma companions from beyond the world and to join them in reverence and refined practice, worn and plain like a rag-robe dhūta, and especially wide in the perfection of giving. All this is hard for the rich and noble to achieve, yet the Lord makes it his ordinary walk. Is he not one who long planted good roots through many lives and, riding the power of his compassionate vow, responds and transforms as an influence? When I first entered the gate of emptiness I did not know the vastness of the Buddhadharma, and thought that to dwell alone, a shadow in the poor mountains and utter ravines, clothed in grass and feeding on trees, holding dry Chan, was the supreme vehicle. But as I drew nearer to the great teaching day by day, reading the Avataṃsaka and beholding Samantabhadra’s wondrous conduct — that there is no kind in which he does not manifest a body and no matter that is not Buddha-work — then, because he does not forsake a single being, I saw the vastness of the Buddha’s compassion; and because he does not abandon a mote or a hair, I came to know the depth of the Dharma-realm. From this, whenever I face officials and speak with them, I no longer probe the dark and embody the wondrous, but only take the awakening to one’s own mind and the wide practice of the ten thousand practices: even the words of conventional truth and the means of livelihood all accord with the right Dharma. This is what is meant by the ground of the principle of reality admitting not a mote of dust, while at the gate of present affairs not a single dharma is abandoned. As for those who idly admire empty fashions and talk loftily of casting off their shoes while glued fast to greed and folly, entangled in the ways of the world — and those who dwell in the world’s net while their will goes beyond the dust, darkening the mind in a far-off region like a lotus rising from the mud, gleaming and unstained — how can they be of the same stalk and root? Thus one knows that although Buddha-nature is one, the habit-defilements are thick or thin, and there is the difference of delusion and awakening. So when we speak of seeds: what springs from greed and anger is nourished by greed and anger; what springs from prajñā is nourished by prajñā. When prajñā is deep, greed and anger are thin; when prajñā appears, greed and anger dissolve. It is as when the wondrous transforms into the rotten and the rotten into the wondrous: the substance is one and the function differs, and by this sage and commoner are divided. When the understanding of the mind is vast, the body cannot confine it; when one sees the Dharma-realm as empty, the ten thousand existents cannot obstruct one. The reason the accomplished man is not entangled in feeling is that his wisdom prevails and his habits are thin. Hence the men of old who awakened the mind took the long river as curds and turned the great earth into gold — what other art was there? Only gaining the wonder of one’s own mind and filling the measure of the Dharma-realm, because outside the mind there is no dharma. The Lord has carved the great commentary on the Huayan at Mount Jizu; in this he has his attainment. Only the roads are barred, and there is no great master of the lineage to open the Lord’s brow-eye; hence the Lord’s will longs for the world beyond and he wishes to travel far and visit good teachers, but is held fast by worldly things and cannot. My own thought is otherwise. If the Lord can sit in stillness and contemplate the mind, then when the six senses melt away the void will perish; and if he sees the Dharma-realm clearly, then mountains and rivers are no barrier. He will see the Flower Store in the tip of a hair and gather the Pure Land into a mote of dust; without moving a step he will walk through the ten directions, and without rising from his seat he will serve all Buddhas. This is the natural endowment of self-nature, complete from the beginning, and never borrowed from without. Moreover the Lord has land: with the breadth of its mountains and rivers and the multitude of its people, let him simply extend his Buddha-mind and teach and transform them. It is said: When one family is humane, a whole state rises to humanity. Let the Lord by his sincere devotion move things and by Buddha-work transform the people, so that every household knows and every door understands, each man knows there is a Buddha and each mind knows there is compassion; then without command the people follow and without awe the people submit, happy and content, feeding their children and drumming on their bellies, and in the far border wilds the manner of a Buddha-land flows wide. The Lord will sit like a lotus and dwell upright in the Land of Bliss, and the government of high antiquity will be within his palm — why then labor to cross mountains and rivers and look on floating light and bubble shadows as the ultimate Buddha-work? From the gentleman I know that the Lord, dwelling in a remote corner among the eight difficulties, must be a responsive body of compassionate vow. I only regret that I am old and cannot carry a single bowl southward to inquire. I look toward his Vaiśālī chamber as though it were at my lashes. I wish to form a bond with the Lord for another age; in the three assemblies of the Dragon Flower I am sure I shall know the Lord as a Buddha-son among officials in the last age of Śākyamuni. Will the Lord not take this to heart?
Record of the Origin of the Long-Eared Dingguang Buddha of Faxiang Temple

The mountains and waters of Hangzhou are the finest under heaven. Ancient sages showed their traces there, and the banner poles within sight of one another stand like a forest — there is no second such place in the realm. Faxiang Temple lies below the South High Peak, deep and far withdrawn, its groves dense, its springs and rocks clear and strange; formerly men rarely reached it. In the Five Dynasties a rare monk hid there, and afterward it became a bodhimaṇḍa. The Master’s name was Xingzhen; he was a son of the Chen family of Quanzhou in Fujian. His mother dreamed she swallowed the sun and conceived; the Master at birth had a strange appearance, his two ears hanging to his shoulders and long enough below to tie at the jaw, and all men thought him strange. At seven he did not speak, and someone pointed and said: Is this child mute? The Master at once opened his mouth and said: Not meeting a master, one only knocks one’s forehead open for nothing. Growing up he left home and studied with Chan Master Xuefeng Cun until he awakened. Then he went on pilgrimage to Siming and hid in the mountains, teaching the Dharma for ghosts and spirits, so that the gods scattered flowers and apes and birds offered fruit. Then he left the mountains and came to Qiantang, hiding at Yingxiu Hollow below the South High Peak. At first there was no water there; when the Master arrived and planted his staff, a spring burst forth. He begged food in the market, and all men found him strange. Children followed him in crowds; seeing his long ears, they pulled them left and right, and the Master turned with them, only smiling foolishly. When asked what work was best to do, the Master said: Doing good deeds can cover a hundred uglinesses. In the third year of Qianyou, on the birthday of the Loyal and Excellent King of Wuyue, monks were fed at Yongming Temple, and Chan Master Zhijue Shou was then opening the great Dharma. The Master came to the assembly covered with scabies and sores and went straight to the seat of honor, and all the assembly disliked him; the King saw him and was greatly disrespectful, and sent him away. He went straight back to the mountains and sat calmly in a room. When the meal was done the King asked Shou: Today we fed monks; has any holy monk descended? Shou said: The long-eared monk is the responsive body of the ancient Buddha Dingguang. The King repented and hurried in his carriage to pay reverence, saying: Your disciple is a common man of fleshly eye and did not know the ancient Buddha; I beg to repent. The Master said: Amitābha is talkative. And with these words he sat and passed away. The King returned to pay reverence to Shou, and Shou too passed away. For this the King built the temple and kept the Master’s flesh body, which survives to this day. The King was moved, and reporting the affairs of both Masters to the throne, asked for posthumous titles: Yongming was granted Great Master Zongzhao, and the Master Great Master Zonghui. Alas, when the Buddha taught the Dharma he often spoke of the five hundred years after, when the semblance Dharma would be spoiled and living beings turbid and evil, hardest of all to teach; and he said: I will send transformed men to open and show the Dharma everywhere to all beings, expounding this Dharma and liberating them. Thus one knows that reverse and forward conduct are both the great authority’s manifestations, skillful means for benefiting beings; whether speaking or silent, nothing but the proclamation of the supreme Dharma. That these two Masters appeared at the same time may be known from this. Yongming, grieving that in the last age nature and marks are hard to make clear, set up the Mirror of the School to lay bare the purport of the one mind, so that none who saw or heard failed to leap in. The long-eared one benefited beings by his strange appearance, and from first to last had no dharma to speak; only by the samādhi of compassionate mind did he gather and transform beings. Because birth and death have love as their root, and men and women are the root of love, he wished to cure love with love; hence he caused beings without children to have their prayers always answered. To this day there is no childless man in the world who does not pray to him, and the prayer is always answered, swift as echo and shadow. This doctrine of not speaking has its teaching blazing, while the bodhimaṇḍa is calm and the incense and fire continue far; so to the very end of the realm of beings, while the root of love is not exhausted, the sound of the Dharma will continue. Can one not believe it? This is the record.
